Computerized by I-Shima and collated by T-Hayashi for the Ikari Project—

The Adyar Library edition is denoted by "A-" in square brackets within the critical apparatus. The symbol "\" indicates a verb.
As a general rule, the negative prefix (a-/an-) is separated from the main part of the word by a hyphen (e.g., a-mṛta).
When the night of Brahmā had passed and the lotus-born one had awakened,
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged in water.
Delighting in sporting in the water, as in former times during the Kalpas,
he assumed the form of a boar and lifted up the earth.
The Veda is his feet, the sacrificial post his tusks, the sacrifices his teeth, and the altars his mouth;
fire is his tongue, the *darbha* grass his hair, Brahman his head, and he is possessed of great austerity.
The divine one has day and night for his eyes, is adorned with the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs as his earrings,
has clarified butter for his nose, a sacrificial ladle for his snout, and the sound of the Sāman chants for his great voice.
Consisting of righteousness and truth, glorious, honored by his progressive strides,
having penance for his great snout, knees of sacrificial animals, and a majestic form.
He has the Udgātṛ priest for his entrails, the sacrificial fire for his characteristic mark, and seeds, herbs, and great fruits for his seed.
He has the sacrificial altar for his inner self, the sacred mantras for his buttocks, and Soma for his blood.
He has the Vedic altar for his shoulders, the fragrance of the oblation for his scent, and he possesses the momentum of the offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya).
His body was the sacrificial hall (prāgvaṃśa), radiant and endowed with various initiations (dīkṣā).
The great Viṣṇu has the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as his heart, consists of the great mantras of Yoga,
possesses lips beautiful with the Upākarma ceremony, and is adorned by the whirlpools of the Pravargya rite.
He whose path is the movement through various Vedic meters, who has the secret Upaniṣads as his seat,
and who is accompanied by his consort Chāyā, has indeed arisen like a mountain of jewels.
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, beheld the earth— extending to the edge of the sea, with its mountains, groves, and forests—
submerged in the waters of that single ocean.
Having lifted [the earth] with the tip of his tusk out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the primordial god, the great yogi, restored the world once again.
Thus, in ancient times, having assumed the form of the Sacrificial Boar, Viṣṇu, desiring the welfare of all beings, lifted up the goddess Earth when she had sunk into the netherworld of Rasātala.
Having lifted [the waters] and established them in their own respective places,
Madhusūdana divided the waters situated therein according to their proper locations.
Sea-salt should be used in the seas, river-salt in the rivers,
salt from ponds in the ponds, and salt produced from lakes in the lakes.
He created the seven netherworlds (pātālas), as well as the seven worlds (lokas),
and the various locations for the continents (dvīpas) and the oceans.
The guardians of the places, the guardians of the worlds, the rivers, the mountains, the trees,
the seven sages who know the Dharma, the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, and the gods and demons.
[He created] the Piśācas, Uragas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and humans;
the fourfold host of beings beginning with domestic animals, birds, and wild beasts;
as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and various kinds of sacrifices.
Thus the Lord Varāha, having created this world with its moving and non-moving beings,
departed for that destination of the worlds which is unknown.
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed for his unknown destination, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me?"
"I shall go to Kaśyapa and ask him; he will explain it to me without doubt, for that great sage is constantly concerned with my welfare."
Having thus made this resolution, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman, went to see Kaśyapa; and Kaśyapa beheld her.

Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her face resembled the autumnal moon; she was beautiful with a lovely brow marked by a swarm of bees, and her auspicious lower lip was the color of the bandhujīva flower.
She possessed beautiful eyebrows, very fine teeth, a lovely nose, and arched brows;
she had a neck like a conch-shell, closely set thighs, and full thighs and hips.
Her two breasts shone forth, being symmetrical, full, and close together.
Resembling the frontal globes of Indra’s elephant and possessing a luster like that of refined gold.
His two arms were as tender as lotus stalks, his hands resembled young sprouts;
his thighs were like pillars of gold, and his knees were well-concealed and closely set.
Her shanks are hairless and perfectly symmetrical, and her feet are exceedingly beautiful; her hips are firm, and her waist is like that of a lion’s cub.
Her copper-colored nails were radiant with luster, her form was captivating to all minds,
and with her constant glances, she made the quarters of the sky appear as if filled with blue lotuses.
The goddess, making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance,
was dressed in very fine white garments and adorned with the finest jewels.
With the placement of her feet, she made the earth appear as if adorned with lotuses;
endowed with beauty and youth, she stood before him with modesty.
Seeing her approach and having honored her, Kaśyapa then said to her, O lady of beautiful hips: "That which was in your heart has been understood by me."
"O Earth, O large-eyed goddess, go to Janārdana;
he will tell you in its entirety how your steadfastness shall come to be."
O lady of auspicious countenance, O lovely-limbed one, by means of meditative yoga and through his grace, I have learned through him that he dwells in the Ocean of Milk for your sake.
Having been addressed in this manner and having honored Kaśyapa,
the Earth then departed for the Milky Ocean, the sea of Kṣīroda, in order to see Keśava.
She beheld that ocean of nectar, enchanting with its moonbeams,
and agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the agitation of the wind.
It was like another hundred-peaked Himalaya, appearing as a second circle of the earth.
With its moving hands of waves, it seems as if calling out to the earth.
By those very [deeds], he was made as if constantly attaining whiteness in the moon,
while his every stain was removed by Hari dwelling within him.
Therefore, he who maintains a very white, powerful body— pale, moving through the sky, inaccessible [to others], and dwelling in the lower regions— [is Viṣṇu].
Rich with sapphire, blue, and tawny hues, the sky appeared as if inverted;
it was filled as if with a multitude of forests produced by rows of fruit-bearing trees.
Indeed, seeing that [ocean] which was exceedingly vast in its expanse like the slough of the serpent Śeṣa,
he beheld there the abode of Keśava situated in its midst.
In that [palace], he beheld Madhusūdana reclining on his remaining couch— a bed whose dimensions were beyond description and whose splendor was beyond description.
His lotus-face is difficult to discern even by the rays of the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
it possesses the brilliance of a hundred moons and the splendor of ten thousand suns.
Clad in yellow garments, imperturbable, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
and resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and two earrings.
His pair of feet was being massaged by Lakṣmī with her beautiful palms, and he was being served on all sides by weapons that had assumed embodied forms.
Having seen that lotus-eyed slayer of Madhu, he prostrated before him,
touching the ground with his knees, and then addressed him.
"O Lord Viṣṇu, I, who had gone to the depths of the netherworld (rasātala), have been raised up by you and established in my own place out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
"O Lord of Gods, what indeed will be my support now in this matter?
Having been addressed thus by that goddess, the God spoke these words.
O Earth, the virtuous who delight in the conduct of their caste and stage of life, and who are solely devoted to the scriptures, will support you; upon them your burden has been placed.
Having been addressed in this manner, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods:
"O Eternal One, declare the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O destroyer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods!
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; O Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, possessed of great strength and prowess!
O Viṣṇu, beyond the senses, difficult to cross over, O God who wields the Śārṅga bow; O Varāha, O Bhīma, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person!
O Hiraṇyakeśa, Viśvākṣa, embodiment of sacrifice, stainless one;
O Lord of the Field, the Knower of the Field, and the God of gods, whose arrow is the ocean of waters!
O inconceivable one who carries the mantras through the mantras, whose body is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
you are the cause of the creation and destruction of this entire world.
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons;
O Viṣvaksena, O Nectar, O Space, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O you who are to be known as the nourisher of the great, O bestower of fearlessness upon all,
O most excellent one, O sinless one, O cloud-like one, O creator of the universe!
O nourisher of the waters, O abode, O consciousness, O support, O inactive one;
O teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, O ancient and supreme Person!
O Dhruva, O Imperishable One, O Most Subtle Lord, O Compassionate toward Your Devotees, O Purifier! You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of those who discourse upon Brahman.
Likewise, O Supreme Person, you are the goal for those who have known what is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Lord Vācaspati.
[He who is] the Subrahmaṇya, the unassailable, the army of wealth, the bestower of wealth,
endowed with the power of great yoga, the offspring of Pṛśni, and the one who maintains the radiance.
To Vāsudeva, the Great Soul, the lotus-eyed, the Infallible,
the divine teacher of gods and asuras, the all-pervading Lord, the supreme sovereign of all beings.
"O Blessed One, tell me of Viṣṇu— who has a single form, four arms, and is the cause of the causes of the universe— and also of the eternal duties of the four castes."
"Endowed with the conduct of the stages of life (āśramas), together with their secret doctrines and compendiums"—
having been thus addressed by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth.
Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life (āśramas), along with their secret doctrines and their essential summaries.
O lady with beautiful thighs, sit down upon this excellent golden seat, which shall be the ultimate refuge for those virtuous ones who uphold you.
"Sit comfortably and learn the duties as I proclaim them to you.
Then the Earth, sitting at ease, listened to the Vaiṣṇava duties.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 2.1:
Om! The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—these are the four castes.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, there is the entire collection of rites, beginning with the impregnation and ending at the cemetery, performed with the recitation of mantras.
And their duties are as follows.
For a Brāhmaṇa, [the duty] is teaching.
For a Kṣatriya, there is a constant obligation to bear arms.
For the Vaiśya, cattle-rearing.
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is [the duty].
For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying.
Now, the means of livelihood for these [are as follows].
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and accepting gifts [are the means of livelihood].
For a Kṣatriya, the protection of the earth.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the cultivation of roots are the duties of the Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, all crafts are [permitted].
In times of distress, the next [lower] mode of livelihood is permitted.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion.
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise absence of malice— this is declared to be the common dharma.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 3:
Now, therefore, the duties of the king.
The protection of the subjects.
The establishment of the social classes and stages of life in their respective duties.
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid, suitable for cattle, and endowed with crops.
And [a village] consisting mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
In that regard, he should take refuge in one of the following types of fortresses: a desert, a man-made fort, an earthwork, a water-fort, a forest-fort, or a mountain-fort.
And remaining there, he should appoint the respective village headmen.
[He shall appoint] ten superintendents.
The superintendents of a hundred.
And [he shall appoint] regional governors. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 3.10)
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village.
If he is unable, he should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
If he, too, is unable, he shall report it to the superintendent of a hundred villages.
If he too is unable [to do so], he shall entrust it to the district magistrate.
The regional governor, too, should eliminate wrongdoing with his whole being.
He should employ trustworthy persons over mines, tolls, ferries, elephants, and forests.
Those most virtuous in matters of religious duty.
Those who are skillful in matters of wealth and affairs.
[He should appoint] heroes for the duties of battle.
One should employ fierce [deities] against fierce [enemies].
One should give eunuchs to women.
For the sake of tribute from his subjects, he shall take a sixth part of the grain produced each year.
And from all types of grain.
For animals, gold, and garments, the fine is two hundred [paṇas].
From meat, honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
One should not collect taxes from Brāhmaṇas.
For they are the ones who establish the king's righteousness.
And the king receives a sixth part of the merits and demerits from his subjects.
And from merchandise produced in his own country, he shall take a tenth part as toll.
And from goods obtained in a foreign land, he shall take a twentieth part.
One who evades the place where the toll is collected shall incur the forfeiture of all his property.
Artisans and those who live by their manual labor shall perform one day's work for the king every month.
Visnu Smṛti 3.33: The sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the realm, and the ally are the constituent elements [of the state].
And he shall put to death those who defile it.
He should have spies as his eyes in both his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others.
One should perform the worship of the virtuous.
And he shall put to death those who are wicked.
One should employ conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force against enemies, friends, neutrals, and those in the middle, as is appropriate and at the proper time.
And he should resort to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, and duplicity at the appropriate times.
In the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa, he should set out on his journey.
Or when another person is in distress.
Upon arriving in another country, one should not abandon the customs of that country.
And when attacked by an enemy, he should protect his own kingdom with all his soul.
For kings, there is no duty equal to the sacrifice of one's body in battle.
Those who are killed while protecting cows, Brahmins, kings, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, partake in the heavenly world.
And for the purpose of protecting the integrity of the social classes (*varṇa*).
Upon the conquest of another's city, the king should install there a member of that [conquered] family.
One should not exterminate the royal family.
Except in the case of a royal family that is not of noble lineage.
One should avoid addiction to hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
And [the rules regarding] verbal abuse and physical assault [are as follows].
One should not cause the loss of wealth.
One should not cut off the primary doors [of the lineage].
One should not shower gifts upon an unworthy recipient.
He should take everything from the mines.
Having found a treasure-trove, one should give half of it to Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause the second half to enter the casket.
Having found a treasure-trove, a Brāhmaṇa may take it all.
A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to the Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself.
But a Vaiśya shall give a fourth part to the king, half to the Brāhmaṇas, and take a fourth part for himself.
And a Śūdra, having divided what he has acquired into twelve parts, shall give five shares to the king, five shares to the Brāhmaṇas, and take two shares for himself.
If it is known that [the food] was not offered [to the deity], one should confiscate everything.
VisnuSm 3.63: From what has been buried by themselves, they should give a twelfth part to the king, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas.
One who claims that what was deposited by another was deposited by oneself shall incur a fine equal to the value of that deposit.
The king shall protect the wealth of minors, the destitute, and women.
Having recovered property stolen by thieves, he shall restore it all to people of all castes.
And if he cannot obtain it from his own treasury, he should give it from [the king's] storehouse itself.
One should pacify the afflictions caused by fate through means such as rites of propitiation (*śānti*), blessings (*svastyayana*), and protective measures (*upāya*).
And he shall ward off attacks from the armies of others by means of constant practice with weapons.

One should choose as a domestic priest (purohita) one who is well-versed in the meaning of the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and the Dharmaśāstras, of noble birth, free from physical defects, and devoted to austerity.
He should appoint as assistants those who are pure, free from greed, attentive, and endowed with the requisite capacity for all matters.
He himself should preside over legal proceedings in the company of learned Brāhmaṇas.
When presiding over legal proceedings, he should appoint either a Brāhmaṇa.

Viṣṇu Smṛti 3.74: The king should appoint as members of his assembly those who are endowed with [noble] birth, conduct, and religious observances; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend; and who cannot be subverted by desire, anger, fear, greed, or other motives related to the matter at hand.
And the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer in all his affairs.
One should constantly worship the gods and the Brahmins.
One should be a servant of the elderly.
And one who performs sacrifices for others.
And in his kingdom, no Brāhmaṇa shall perish, afflicted by hunger.
Nor indeed anyone else who is devoted to virtuous deeds.
And he should bestow land upon Brāhmaṇas.

To those to whom he bestows it, he should give a document—written on cloth or a copper plate, inscribed with his own seal, and containing the names of their descendants, the dimensions of the land, and a description of the grant’s boundaries—for the purpose of informing future kings.
And one must not seize land that has been given by another.
He should bestow all gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
But one should protect oneself from all sides.
And he should be pleasant to behold.
And one who possesses mantras that destroy poison and act as an antidote.
One should not consume anything that has not been examined.
One should speak with a smile as a prelude.
Even toward those deserving of execution, one should not knit one's brows in a frown.
And he shall cause punishment to be inflicted upon those deserving of it, in accordance with the nature of their offense.
He should administer punishment correctly.
He should not forgive anyone for a second offense.
There is no one who, failing to observe his own duty, should not be punished by kings.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Daṇḍa moves about fearlessly,
there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
In his own kingdom, he should administer justice through punishment; toward enemies, he should employ severe punishment;
toward friends and affectionate Brahmins, he should be straightforward and endowed with forgiveness.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he subsists by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
The king who finds happiness in the happiness of his subjects and who is grieved by their sorrow is endowed with fame in this world and, after death, is glorified in heaven.
The particle of dust situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice, known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [transitional particles] make one *likṣā*.
Three of those [mustard seeds] constitute one royal mustard seed (*rāja-sarṣapa*).
Those three [mustard seeds] constitute one white mustard seed (gaura-sarṣapa).
Six of those [rathikas] make one barleycorn (yava).
Three of those [māṣas] constitute one kṛṣṇala.
Five of those [rathikas] make one māṣa.
Twelve of those [māṣas] make one akṣa-ardha.
A *suvarṇa* consists of five *akṣas*, which includes four *māṣakas*.
A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together constitute one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those [māṣas] constitute one dharaṇa.
A kārṣāpaṇa consists of one kārṣika of copper.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are recorded as the first amercement (sāhasa);
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand is the highest.
VisnuSm 5.1: Now, all those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin), with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, are liable to capital punishment.
There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa.
He shall banish from his own country a Brāhmaṇa who has been branded.
And in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, he should fashion a headless man upon his forehead.
For drinking liquor, the mark of a tavern flag.
In the case of theft, one's own foot [is the measure].
Visnu Smṛti 5.7: [The mark of] the female organ [is prescribed] for one who has sexual intercourse with the teacher's bed.
Even in other cases involving capital punishment, he should banish the offender with his entire wealth intact and unharmed.
And the king shall put to death those who forge false edicts.
And those who forge documents.
Poison-givers, arsonists, violent robbers, and those who kill women, children, or men.
And those who would steal more than ten jars of grain; ViṣṇuSm 5.12.
In the case of things measured by weight, [the fine shall be] more than one hundred [paṇas].
And those who are of low birth who might desire sovereignty.
And those who destroy bridges.
And those who forcibly provide shelter and food to thieves.
Except in the case of inability on the part of the king.
A woman whose husband is incapable [of fulfilling her needs] and one who transgresses him.
If a person of lower caste should commit an offense against one of higher caste by means of a particular limb, that very limb of his shall be cut off.
One who sits upon the same seat [as a teacher] or marks his hip with a sectarian sign shall be banished.
Having spat, one should rinse the mouth until it is free from both lips.
And one who habitually voids excrement is deprived of his anus.
And one who reviles others is called *vijihva*.
Visnu Smṛti 5.24: The king shall cause hot oil to be poured into the mouths of those who, out of arrogance, provide instruction on the Dharma.
And for maliciously mentioning someone's name or caste, a ten-finger-long peg shall be driven into his body.
One who speaks falsely regarding what has been heard, or regarding country, caste, or occupation, shall be fined two hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
In the case of those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise disabled, even if they speak the truth, they shall be fined two kārṣāpaṇas.
One who insults his gurus shall pay a fine of two hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
But when an accusation involving a sin causing loss of caste is made against another, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
For one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka), the middle amercement is prescribed.
In the case of insulting those who are learned in the three Vedas, or groups of people belonging to various castes.
And for [the theft of] a village or a district, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For an insult involving a physical deformity, the fine shall be one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
But when it is joined with the mother, it is the highest [merit].
For insulting someone of the same caste, one shall be fined twelve paṇas.
For reviling one of a lower caste, the penance is six [days].
If one insults a person of a higher caste at the appropriate time, the punishment shall be equal to the value of that [insult].
Or three kārṣāpaṇas.
But when the *śukta-vākya* is recited, it is exactly the same.
A man who commits adultery with a woman of his own caste shall be punished with the highest amercement.
In approaching a woman of a lower caste, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
And [the same penance applies] for sexual intercourse with a cow.
One who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste (antyā) is to be executed.
For sexual intercourse with a female animal, one shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
And he who gives away a maiden without disclosing her defects.
And he should maintain her.
One who says of a woman who is not corrupt that she is corrupt shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, a cow, or a goat shall have one hand and one foot cut off.
And one who sells meat. VisnuSm 5.49.
One who kills a domestic animal shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
He shall pay its value to the owner of the animal.
One who kills a wild animal shall pay five hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
A killer of birds and a killer of fish shall pay ten kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who injures insects shall pay a kārṣāpaṇa.
But one who cuts down a tree that bears fruit when it is in season incurs the highest amercement.
One who cuts down a tree that provides flowers or fruit incurs the middle amercement.
One who cuts creepers, shrubs, or climbing plants shall pay one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
One [day and night] for cutting grass.
And all [the sons] shall receive that [property] from its owners according to their respective shares of origin.
One who threatens with his hand shall pay a fine of ten kārṣāpaṇas.
With the foot [of the staff], twenty [times].
If [one strikes] with wood, the first amercement.
With a stone, the middle amercement.
The highest [merit] is attained by means of a weapon. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.64)
For the theft of a foot, hair, a garment, or a hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas.
One who causes pain without drawing blood shall pay a fine of thirty-two paṇas.
With blood, one incurs sixty-four [births].
In the case of breaking a hand, a foot, or a tooth, or in the case of cutting off an ear or the nose, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
In cases of restraining someone's movements, food, or speech, as well as in the act of inflicting a blow; Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.69.
And for the breaking of the eyes, neck, arms, thighs, or shoulders, the highest [amercement] shall be imposed.
The king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives one who pierces both eyes.
Or he may perform exactly that same [rite].
VisnuSm 5.73: For many who strike a single person, the punishment for each shall be double that which has been prescribed.
For those standing nearby who do not run toward one crying out, and for those passing by, [the same penalty applies].
And all those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses incurred for their recovery.
And those who cause pain to domestic animals.
One who steals a cow, a horse, a camel, or an elephant shall have one hand and one foot cut off.
One who steals goats or sheep, and one who acts as a single-handed assassin.
One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value.
And one who steals grain.
One who steals more than fifty units of gold, silver, or clothing shall be punished with mutilation.
He shall be fined eleven times the value of that deficiency.

Visnu Smriti 5.83: One who steals articles made of thread, cotton, cow-dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, grass, salt, clay, ashes, birds, fish, ghee, oil, meat, honey, split pulses, bamboo, earthenware, or metal vessels shall be fined three times their value.
And [the same applies] to cooked foods. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.84)
For the theft of flowers, green plants, shrubs, creepers, climbing vines, or leaves, the fine is five kṛṣṇalas.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One who steals gems shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who steals articles not specifically mentioned [in the preceding rules] shall pay a fine equal to their value.
Thieves must be made to restore everything they have stolen to the owner.
Then follows the application of the prescribed punishment for them.
He who gives the wrong path to those for whom the right path must be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who does not offer a seat to a person worthy of a seat [commits an offense].
And one who does not worship those worthy of worship.
And also for neglecting an invitation to a neighboring Brāhmaṇa.
And those who, having invited [others], do not provide them with food.
Likewise, one who has been invited and has replied "so be it," yet does not eat, [should give] a māṣaka of gold.
And for one who provides a dwelling, the food shall be double.
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall pay a fine of sixteen suvarṇas.
For one who causes the loss of caste, the fine is one hundred [paṇas].
One who [drinks] spirituous liquor is to be executed.
For one who defames a Kṣatriya, the fine is half of that.
For one who defiles a Vaiśya, the fine is even half of that.
For one who defames a Śūdra, the first amercement shall be imposed.
One who, out of intentional desire, touches a member of the three higher castes who is not to be touched, shall be put to death.
One should strike a woman in her menses with whips.
One who voids impurities even near a road, a garden, or water shall be fined one hundred paṇas.
And that [impurity] he should cast away.
One who breaks a house, land, wall, or the like, shall be punished with the middle amercement.
And one should employ that [formula].
One who throws an object that causes distress into another's house shall pay one hundred paṇas.
And one who denies a common property.
And one who does not give what has been sent [to him]. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.112)
And one who abandons a father, son, teacher, sacrificial client, or officiating priest, provided they have not fallen from their status.
And one should not abandon them.
Śūdras and those who have renounced the world (pravrajita) are [unfit] to be feeders at rites for the gods or the ancestors.
And one who performs unworthy actions.
And one who breaks into the sea or a house.
One who administers an oath without being authorized is a transgressor.
One who causes the loss of virility in male animals. *Viṣṇu Smṛti* 5.119.
In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is ten paṇas.
And whoever should intervene between those two, for him there shall be the highest amercement.
And for one who practices fraud regarding weights and measures.
And for one who speaks falsely regarding what is not a counterfeit [article].
And for one who sells counterfeit goods.
When merchants, having come together, withhold their merchandise at an improper price.
And for those who sell [the items] individually.
If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay that price along with the profit.
And the king shall fine him one hundred paṇas.
Whatever loss occurs to one who does not purchase what has been sold shall belong to the purchaser alone.
For one who sells what is prohibited by the king, there shall be the forfeiture of that [property].
A ferryman who collects a land-toll shall be fined ten paṇas.
A boatman, a customs officer, and one who collects tolls [are liable for the sin] of one who follows a student, a forest-dweller, a mendicant, a pregnant woman, or a person visiting a sacred ford.
And he should give that to them.
In gambling, the hands of those who play with fraudulent dice shall be cut off.
For those who gamble with fraudulent devices, the punishment is the cutting off of the thumb.
And for those who break open knots [of property], Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.136.
And for those who commit robbery with violence, the hands shall be cut off.
Visnu Smṛti 5.138: If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not present, the fault lies with the herdsman.
And he shall pay the value of the lost animal to its owner.
One who milks a cow without permission shall pay twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
If a buffalo should cause the destruction of crops, its keeper shall be fined eight māṣas.
The owner [is the one who takes] the offspring of a cow that has no keeper.
But a horse, a camel, or a donkey [is not to be eaten].
If it is a cow, the fine is half of that.
Half of that [is the value] for a goat or a sheep.
If they have already eaten and are sitting down, the fine is double.
In all cases, the owner shall also pay the value of the destroyed crop.
There is no fault [in killing] on a road, in a village, or at the edge of a pasture.
And [one must not study] in an uncovered place.
For a short time. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.150)
And [the meat] of cows that have calved after being set free as *vṛṣabha* (bulls).
But he who employs those of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who has abandoned the life of a renunciant shall perform service for the king.
And a hired servant who abandons his service before the agreed time has expired shall pay the full amount of the wages.
And in the case of a sacrificial fee, he shall pay one hundred paṇas.
Whatever may be lost through his fault, that shall belong to the owner.
Except in the case of an act of God.
If the employer should dismiss the laborer before the term is completed, he must pay him the full value of his wages.
And one hundred paṇas to the king.
Except in the case of a fault on the part of the hired servant.
He who gives away a daughter who has already been promised to another shall be punished like a thief.
Except in the case of a fault in the bridegroom.
Abandoning a wife who is without fault; Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.163.
And [he should not eat] with his wife.
If one purchases another's property openly without knowing [it belongs to someone else], he is not at fault in that matter.
The owner shall receive the property.
If one should purchase an item that is unexposed to view and of low value, then both the buyer and the seller shall be punished like thieves.
One who misappropriates the property of a corporate body shall be banished.
And he who violates the agreement with them.
He shall be made to pay to the creditor the wealth along with the interest on the deposit and the stolen property.
And he shall be punished by the king like a thief.
And he who says that something was deposited which was not deposited; ||| VisnuSm 5.172 ||| he who says that something was deposited which was not deposited.
Having punished the violator of a boundary with the highest amercement, he shall have the boundary re-established.
One who eats food that is unfit to be eaten because it causes loss of caste shall be banished.
One who sells what is unfit for consumption or what is forbidden to be sold, as well as one who destroys an image of a deity, shall be punished with the highest amercement.
A physician who practices deceitfully toward persons of the highest status.
In the case of middling offenses, the middle fine shall be imposed.
Among animals, the first [is the expiation].
One who does not give what has been promised shall be compelled to pay it and be fined the first amercement.
For false witnesses, the confiscation of all their property shall be carried out.
And for members of the court who subsist on bribes, [the fine is one thousand].
He who, without having released from one person land measuring at least a *go-carma* that has been mortgaged to him, should bestow it upon another, is to be put to death.
If it is less than sixteen suvarṇas, he shall be fined [the amount].
If a man eats for one year whatever fruit has been produced [by a gift],
that earth— whether it be small or large— is considered by him to be as vast as a cow-hide.
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
the one whose enjoyment of it was carried out without force has the benefit of it.
But when property has been enjoyed for a long time with a clear title, the possessor acquires it;
it can never be taken away from him.

But whatever property was enjoyed by the father in accordance with custom and according to dharma, when he has died, no objection can be raised against that; for it belongs to him by virtue of such enjoyment.
But land that has been enjoyed by three persons in due order,
even in the absence of a written document, may be acquired there by a fourth person.
In the case of killing those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins,
as well as elephants, horses, and other such creatures, the killer incurs no guilt.
One may indeed slay, without hesitation, an assailant approaching, even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brahmin deeply learned in the Vedas.
In the killing of an *ātatāyin* (one who comes to kill), no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer;
whether done openly or in secret, it is fury that meets fury.
One who raises a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who raises his hand to pronounce a curse;
one who kills by means of the Atharva-veda; and a slanderer among kings.
One should know that there are seven types of assailants: one who violates his wife, those who seize his fame or wealth, and others who take away his dharma or his purpose.
O Earth, I have described to you this method of punishment for all offenses in brief, as it would be too extensive to detail at length.
In other offenses as well, having ascertained the caste, wealth, and age [of the offender],
the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brāhmaṇas.

One who releases a person liable to punishment from that punishment shall incur a fine double the amount of the original penalty. Furthermore, an official appointed to oversee justice who inflicts punishment upon those who do not deserve it is the lowest of men.
In whose city there is no thief, no one who covets another's wife, and no one of wicked speech—[that king attains the world of Indra].
That king who does not inflict punishment on the perpetrator of violence nor on the murderer shall partake in the world of Śakra.
Now, the creditor of superior status shall receive from the debtor of inferior status the amount of wealth as it was lent.
Two, three, four, five, and ten percent [of the principal] per month, according to the order of the social classes (varṇa).
Or all castes may pay the interest as it was agreed upon by themselves.
Even that which has not been performed becomes as prescribed when a year has elapsed.
When there is enjoyment of a pledge, there is no interest.
Except in the case of damage caused by the king or an act of God, the creditor shall not recover a pledge that has been destroyed.
Even when the night has entered its final increase.
Immovable property may not be pledged, except by a specific agreement.
Whatever immovable property has been given solely for the purpose of recovering the money received, that shall be returned once the money received has been recovered.
When the principal amount lent is being paid back, interest on it ceases to accrue from that point forward for one who does not accept it.
The maximum interest on gold is double the principal.
For grain, the interest is threefold.
For a garment, it is fourfold.
For sugar, the fine is eightfold.
The offspring belongs to the female and the cattle.
There is no time-limit for the sale of fermenting agents, cotton thread, skins, weapons, bricks, and charcoal.
For those not mentioned, the fine is double.
One who recovers a loan that was lent in any manner whatsoever shall not be subject to reproach by the king.
If one being prosecuted should approach the king, he shall be fined an amount equal to that [of the claim].

If the debtor of the superior kind should approach the king, then the debtor of the inferior kind, having been proven in that matter, shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the amount of the debt.
And a debtor who has acquired wealth [to pay] shall give the twentieth part [of that wealth] to the creditor of the highest class.
Visnu Smṛti 6.22: Even if one part [of a claim] is proven against someone who denies everything, he shall pay the whole.
And for that [debt], there are three means of proof: a written document, witnesses, and a formal agreement.
What has been received in the presence of witnesses should be returned in the very same manner, in the presence of witnesses.
When the matter recorded in writing has been entered [into the court], one should cause the document to be read aloud.
In the case of a partial payment or when the document is not present, the debtor shall provide his own written acknowledgment.
If the debtor who received the money has died, renounced the world, or gone abroad, the debt must be paid by his sons or grandsons after twelve years have passed.
Thereafter, those who do not desire [the fruits of their actions] need not perform anything further.
Whether he has sons or is sonless, the heir to the estate shall pay the debt.
One who seizes the wife of a man who is destitute of wealth [is a thief].
A woman does not [incur the debt] created by her husband or her son.
Neither the husband nor the son [shall inherit] property acquired by a woman.
A father does not incur [the sin] committed by his son.
He who remains among those who have not divided their property shall pay the debt contracted by them.
The paternal debt belongs to brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance.
And those who have divided [the inheritance] shall take their shares in proportion to the estate.
The husband of women belonging to the classes of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, or hunters shall pay [the fine].
That which has been acknowledged by word alone must not be withheld from anyone.
And that which was done for the sake of the family.
He who, having received a loan in full, says "I will pay it tomorrow" in a conciliatory manner,
but subsequently fails to repay it out of greed, shall incur interest on that amount.
Suretyship is ordained for the purpose of seeing, for confidence, and for payment;
however, if the first two [types] fail, the debt must be paid by them, and in the case of the latter, even their sons may be made to pay.

If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement made; however, if no specific distinction regarding the share of the debt has been specified among them, the payment shall be made according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever amount a surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor ought to pay that same amount doubled to the surety.
Visnu Smṛti 7:
Now, documentary evidence is of three kinds.
[Transactions] witnessed by the king, witnessed by [other] witnesses, and those without witnesses.
In the royal court, a document executed by a *kāyastha* appointed by the king and marked with the hand-seal of its presiding officer is one witnessed by the king.
Wherever and by whomever it may have been written, if it is signed with their own hands and witnessed by witnesses, it is considered valid.
A document written by one's own hand is valid even without witnesses.
That which is performed under duress is invalid.
All transactions entered into through fraud are indeed void.
Even a case accompanied by witnesses is [rejected] if it is tainted by corrupted actions or marked by corrupt witnesses.
And it must be written by a scribe of such a kind.
And that which is done by a woman, a child, one who is not independent, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is terrified, or one who has been beaten.
That which is not contrary to local custom, whose subject matter and characteristics are clear, and whose sequence and syllables are unimpaired, is authoritative.

One should establish a doubtful document by means of the [social] classes, the marks made by them, the leaves [of the manuscript], and logical arguments, as well as by means of circumstantial evidence corresponding to those [factors].
Wherever a debtor, a creditor, a witness, or even a scribe dies, one should validate that document by means of their own handwriting.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 8: Now, those who are not witnesses.

Viṣṇu Smṛti 8.2: Not [to be examined as witnesses] are the king, a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), a renunciant (pravrajita), a gambler, a thief, one dependent on another, a woman, a child, a violent person, one who is very old, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one accused of a crime, an outcast (patita), one afflicted by hunger or thirst, one in distress, one addicted to vices, and one blinded by passion.
And those who have enemies, friends, or financial interests; those whose misconduct has been observed; those who have committed offenses; and those who have allies.
But he who, though not specifically designated as a witness, comes forward and speaks [in court], is also [a witness].
And a single person is not a witness.
In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, and adultery, witnesses need not be examined for their qualifications.
Now, concerning witnesses. VisnuSm 8.07.

Those born of noble lineage, endowed with good conduct and wealth, performers of sacrifices, ascetics, possessed of sons, knowers of dharma, learned in the Vedas, truthful, and advanced in the three branches of knowledge.
Even a single person, provided he is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and is approved by both parties, [is a suitable witness].
Visnu Smṛti 8.10: When two parties are disputing, the witnesses of the one who has the prior claim should be questioned.
Where, due to the requirements of the case, the burden of proof falls upon the plaintiff, there it shall also fall upon the defendant.
If the designated witness has died or has gone to another country, those who have heard what was stated by him are the authority.
A witness is one who has seen [the matter] face-to-face or heard it.
And witnesses are purified by truth.
In cases where there is the killing of those belonging to the [four] castes, [one may speak] with untruth.
To purify that [act], a twice-born man should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
A Śūdra should give a single day's portion of fodder for ten cows.
One should recognize a false witness by a change in natural disposition, a transformation of facial color, and incoherent prattle.
And having summoned the witnesses at sunrise, he should question them after they have taken their oaths.
He should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak."
"Speak the truth," [he says] to a Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya [should be fined] with cattle, seed-grain, and gold.
But for all the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka), [the penance applies] to a Śūdra.
And he should cause the witnesses to hear [the charge].
Those worlds which are for the perpetrators of great sins and those for the perpetrators of minor sins belong also to false witnesses.
And between birth and death, there is the loss of whatever good or evil deeds have been performed.
By truth the sun gives heat.
By truth the moon shines.
By truth the wind blows.
By truth the earth supports [all beings].
By truth, the waters stand firm.
By truth, Agni [is pleased]. VisnuSm 8.32.
And the sky [is established] by truth.
By truth, the gods [are pleased].
By truth, sacrifices [are perfected].
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices.
For those who, though knowing the facts, remain silent and indifferent when called upon as witnesses,
are equal to false witnesses in their sin and also in their punishment.
In this manner, the king shall question the witnesses according to the order of their castes. He whose claim the witnesses declare to be true shall be the victor;
he who speaks otherwise shall certainly suffer defeat.

In a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the testimony of the majority; if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict between virtuous men, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
In whatever legal dispute a false witness should speak untruth, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been performed, it shall be as if unperformed.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 9:
Now, the performance of compacts.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the punishment shall be] according to his pleasure.
In cases of deposits and theft, the value of the object determines the penalty.
In all matters concerning property, one should calculate the value in terms of gold.
In that case, if the amount is less than a *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding blades of *dūrvā* grass in his hand.
A handful of sesame seeds deficient by two kṛṣṇalas [is the measure].
If it is deficient by three kṛṣṇalas, he shall pay a hand full of silver.
If it is less than four kṛṣṇalas, the fine shall be one suvarṇa.
One who takes five *kṛṣṇalas* from land raised by the plow [is a thief].
If it is less than half a suvarṇa, a leather bag (kośa) should be given as a fine for a Śūdra.
After that, one should administer any one of the ordeals—the balance, fire, water, or poison—according to what is appropriate for the case.
When the amount in dispute is double [the value], the rules for the transaction of agreements as previously stated apply to the Vaiśya.
For a Kṣatriya, it is threefold.
In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be fourfold, with the exception of the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).
One should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to undergo ordeal by the balance.
Except for an action bound by a future time or occasion.
In the place of the *kośa* ordeal, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by touching earth taken from a furrow.
In cases where a fault has been previously observed, even if the matter is trivial, one should administer one of the divine ordeals.
Even in a matter of great importance, one should not disclose a secret that is known among the virtuous.
The plaintiff shall carry his head uncovered.
And one who is accused shall undergo an ordeal.
In cases of treason against the king or acts of violence, [the ordeal may be performed] even without the shaving of the head.
A balance scale should be provided for women, Brahmins, the disabled, the infirm, and the sick.
And that [smell] does not waft when the wind is not blowing.
Fire should not be given to lepers, the infirm, or blacksmiths.
And during the autumn and summer seasons.
Poison should not be administered to those suffering from leprosy, to those with bilious disorders, or to Brāhmaṇas.
And during the rainy season. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 9.28)
Water [is not to be offered] for those afflicted by phlegm or disease, for the timid, for those suffering from asthma or coughing, nor for those who live by water.
And [the same applies] during the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 9.30)
A treasury must not be given to atheists.
Nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence.
Having summoned one who has fasted and bathed with his clothes on at sunrise,
he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 10: Now, the ordeal of the balance (dhaṭa).
It should be four cubits in height and two cubits in width.
In that case, the balance-beam, made from a strong tree, shall be five cubits long and provided with two strings at both ends.
And she shall be maintained by whichever one among the goldsmiths or the brazier-casters [is available].
And there, he should place the person undergoing the ordeal on one scale, and a counterweight such as a stone on the second.
Having made both the counterweight and the man equal in weight and well-marked, one should cause the man to descend.
And one should take up the ordeal by balance according to the established rule.
And one who maintains a scale for weighing goods.
Those worlds that are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those worlds for false witnesses— those same worlds belong to the one who handles the scales falsely while weighing them.
By words synonymous with "dharma," you are called the *dhaṭa*. O *dhaṭa*, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed upon you;
therefore, you ought to deliver him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Then he should place that man once again upon the scale;
if, when weighed, he increases in weight, then he is purified according to the law.
In the event of the breaking of the sling or the snapping of the cords, one should have the man weighed again;
for in this way, there arises a certain knowledge that leads to a definitive verdict.
Visnu Smṛti 11: Now, the fire.
One should draw seven circles with an interval of sixteen finger-breadths each.
Then, he should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands of the person who is facing east with both arms extended.
And one should wrap those [fingers], together with both hands, with a thread.
Then, he should place there a ball of iron, glowing with the color of fire, weighing exactly fifty palas.
Taking that [staff], he should walk neither too quickly nor too slowly, placing his feet within the prescribed circles.
Then, having passed beyond the seventh circle, he should drop a lump of iron upon the ground.
One whose hands have been burnt anywhere should be declared impure;
however, that man who is not burnt at all shall be considered pure.
But if one should cause [the metal] to fall out of fear, or if it is burnt and cannot be discerned,
he shall have that iron brought back again because the ordeal has not been cleared according to the rule.
At the very outset, one should examine his hands as they handle the crushed grains;
then, having consecrated them with mantras, one should place a ball of iron upon his hands.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O Agni, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Viṣṇu Smṛti 12: Now, regarding water.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 12.01. Now, regarding water.
In water that is free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like.
In that regard—having grasped the knees of another man who is free from disease and hatred and who has submerged himself up to the navel—one should enter the consecrated water.
And at that same time, another man should discharge an arrow with a bow that is neither too harsh nor too soft.
And another man should quickly fetch that arrow for him.
Among them, he who is not seen is proclaimed pure;
otherwise, he would be impure even upon the sight of a single limb.
O Water, you move within all beings like a witness;
you alone know those waters which human beings do not perceive.
"Accused in this legal proceeding, this mortal man sinks into you."
Therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 13:
Now, the ordeal by poison.
All kinds of poisons are not to be given.
Except for that which originates from the Himālaya mountains and the horn of the Śārṅga deer.
And one should give seven barley grains soaked in clarified butter to the person accused.
If the poison is digested easily, free from violent onset or exhaustion,
then recognizing him as pure, one should release him at the end of the day.
O Poison, because of your nature as poison and your treacherous character, you are cruel toward all embodied beings;
you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
VisnuSm 14:
Now, therefore, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should drink three handfuls of water from their bath-water.
Saying, "This was not done by me," he faces the installed deity.
