One should know him to be impure; conversely, he is pure in the opposite case. A righteous king should treat a man who has proven pure in an ordeal as a virtuous person.
VisnuSm 15: Now, there are twelve kinds of sons.
The first is the legitimate son (aurasa), begotten by oneself upon one's own wedded wife who has undergone the purificatory rites.
A son begotten by a man of the highest caste who is a sapinda upon a woman duly appointed is the second type, known as the "soil-born" (kṣetraja).
The son of an appointed daughter is the third.
She who is given by her father with the stipulation, "The son who is born of her shall be my son," is a *putrikā*.
Even without the formal rite for an appointed daughter (*putrikā-vidhi*), a girl who has been given away in marriage and is without brothers is indeed considered an *appointed daughter*.
The fourth is the paunarbhava (the son of a remarried woman).
A woman who has been consecrated again with unbroken grains is called a *punarbhū*.
But a woman who has previously belonged to another man, even if she has not been consecrated by marriage, may be taken again.
The fifth is the kānīna (the son of an unmarried woman).
One who is begotten by a woman who has not been consecrated through the marriage rites while she is still in her father's house.
And that [offering] belongs to the one who took her hand in marriage.
And the one born in secret in the house is the sixth.
He belongs to the one from whose bed he was born.
The son taken with the bride (sahoḍha) is the seventh.
If a pregnant woman undergoes the sacramental rite, the son born to her [is considered initiated].
And that [offering] belongs to the one who took her hand in marriage.
And the adopted son (dattaka) is the eighth.
And he belongs to those by whose mother and father he was given.
And the ninth is the purchased slave.
And he belongs to him by whom he was purchased.
One who comes of his own accord is the tenth.
And he belongs to the one to whom he has come.
The eleventh is the *apaviddha* (the abandoned).
VisnuSm 15-25: One who has been abandoned by his father and mother.
And he [the debt] belongs to him by whom it was received.
And wherever he may have been begotten, he is the twelfth [in the order of sons].
Among these, each preceding one is superior to the next.
He alone is the inheritor of the estate.
And he should support others as well.
For those who have not been married, one should perform the sacramental rite in accordance with their own wealth.
But those who are outcasts, eunuchs, or afflicted with incurable diseases or physical deformities shall not receive a share.
They shall be maintained by those who inherit their property.
And their legitimate sons (aurasa) are the heirs to their shares.
But not for one who has fallen [from his caste].
But when a patanīya act has been committed, those born subsequently [lose their caste].
And those born of women in the inverse order of castes (pratiloma) are non-partakers of the inheritance.
His sons [have a claim] even to the property of the grandfather.
Those who take hold of his shoulders must support him.
And he who takes the wealth shall also offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Even among women married to one man, the son of one is indeed the son of all.
And [the same applies] to brothers born of one [mother].
Even in the absence of paternal wealth, a son should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Since a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-existent One himself.
The father pays off his debt to him and attains immortality,
provided that he beholds the face of his son while the son is born and living.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter's son;
for even a daughter's son rescues his father who has no son, just like a grandson.
Sons born of women of the same caste as their father are of the same caste.
From women of the same caste as the mother, those born in the direct order of castes are of the same caste as their mothers.
Those born from women of inverse order (pratiloma) are despised by the noble ones.
In that regard, the son of a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is an Āyogava.
The Pulkasa and the Māgadha are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by Vaiśya and Śūdra fathers respectively.
The Caṇḍāla, the Vaidehaka, and the Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇī woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya, respectively.
And the mixed castes resulting from further intermixture are innumerable.
The descent into the arena is for the Āyogavas.
The occupation of the Pulkasas is hunting.
The occupation of the Māgadhas is the performance of praise.
And the occupation of executing those condemned to death belongs to the Caṇḍālas.
The protection of women and their livelihood are the duties of the Vaidehakas.
The management of horses and chariots is the duty of the Sūtas.
For Caṇḍālas, the specific rules are: dwelling outside the village and wearing the clothes of the deceased.
And for all of them, marriage is with those of the same caste.
And the misappropriation of the wealth of one's own father.
These castes born of intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own respective occupations.
The self-sacrifice of the body, unconditionally offered for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of cows,
as well as [dying] in the protection of women, children, and others, is the cause of liberation for those of the outer castes.
If the father divides the property among his sons, he may exercise his own will regarding wealth acquired by himself.
But in the case of ancestral property, the ownership of father and son is equal.
The brothers who have been divided from their father shall give a share to one born after the division.
The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to his wife.
In his absence, it goes to the daughter.
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the father.
In the absence of that [son], it goes to the mother.
In his absence, it goes to the brother.
In his absence, it goes to the brother's son.
In the absence of that, it goes to the kinsman.
In the absence of those, it goes to a kinsman (sakulya).
In his absence, it goes to one who studied together with him.
In the absence of that [heir], the property goes to the king, with the exception of the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa.
The property of Brāhmaṇas belongs to Brāhmaṇas.
The preceptor shall take the property of a forest hermit (vānaprastha).
Or a disciple. Viṣṇu Smṛti 17.16; siṣyo vā.
But one who is reunited with another shall inherit from that reunited kinsman, and a uterine brother from his uterine brother;
he shall both give and receive a share for one born or for one deceased.

That which is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire; that given on account of supersession by another wife; that given by a kinsman; the bride-price; and the subsequent gift—these constitute the property of a woman.
In the case of the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, when she has died childless, [the property] belongs to her husband.
And in the remaining cases, the father shall take [the property].
Visnu Smṛti 17.21: In all these cases, whatever property belongs to a woman who has given birth shall go to her daughter.
Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide that; those who do divide it fall from their caste.
In the case of those who have multiple fathers, however, the allotment of shares is according to the father;
whatever paternal inheritance belongs to a person, he shall take that, and not the other.
Visnu Smṛti 18.1: If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons born of the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts.
In that case, the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife shall take four shares.
The son of a Kṣatriya woman [inherits] three.
The son of a Vaiśya receives two shares.
But the son of a Śūdra woman [inherits] one share.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have three sons, excluding a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into nine parts.
According to the order of the castes, they shall take shares divided into four, three, and two parts respectively.
Excluding the Vaiśya, [the other castes] should take four, three, and one [shares] respectively from the estate divided into eight parts.
Excluding the Kṣatriya, [the inheritance] is divided sevenfold: four, two, and one.
Excluding the Brāhmaṇa, [the property] is divided into six parts, three, two, and one [respectively].
In the case of a Kṣatriya father having sons by a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra wife, this same division [of property] applies.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa son shall take four shares.
A Kṣatriya [should wait] for three [days].
Now, if there are a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya [sons] of a Brāhmaṇa father, then the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares out of the estate divided into six parts.
The Vaiśya shall receive two shares.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts.
The Brāhmaṇa, however, shall take four shares.
A Śūdra [should perform] one.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, one a Kṣatriya and the other a Vaiśya, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, shall take three shares.
The Vaiśya shall take two shares.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, one a Kṣatriya and the other a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into four parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, shall take three shares.
A Śūdra [should perform] one. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 18.24)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should have two sons who are a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into three parts.
The Vaiśya, however, shall take two shares.
A Śūdra [should perform] one [oblation]. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 18.27)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa has only one son, then sons born of Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya wives shall all inherit his entire estate.
For a Kṣatriya, [the penance is] that of a Rājanya or a Vaiśya.
For a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya [is the witness].
A Śūdra [shall perform the penance] for a Śūdra.
Among the twice-born, however, a Śūdra son who is the only son shall take half the inheritance.
Whatever destiny awaits the inheritance of one who dies without a son, that same destiny applies here to the second half [of the estate].
The mothers shall take shares in accordance with the shares of their sons.
And unmarried daughters [shall receive shares].
Sons of the same caste as their father shall take equal shares.
They should give the best extra portion to the eldest brother.

Viṣṇu Smṛti 18.38: If there should be two sons born of Brāhmaṇa wives and one son born of a Śūdra wife, then, when the property is divided into nine parts, the two Brāhmaṇa sons shall take eight shares and the Śūdra son shall take one share.

Now, if there should be two sons of a Śūdra woman and one son of a Brāhmaṇa woman, then the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares of the wealth divided into six parts, and the two Śūdra sons shall take two shares.
By this sequence, the apportionment of shares occurs in other cases as well.
If those who were previously divided, living together again, should divide once more, the division there shall be equal; in that case, the right of primogeniture does not exist.
If one acquires property through his own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
that which is obtained by his own effort he need not give away against his will.

But when one recovers ancestral property that had not been previously obtained, he shall not share it with his sons; likewise, property acquired by himself without desire [for gain] shall not be shared with them.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of person and property, pasture grounds, and books are not to be divided.
VisnuSm 19.01: One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra.
A twice-born man must not [teach] a Śūdra.
Sons shall carry out the funeral rites for their father and mother.
Śūdras shall not [serve] a twice-born man, even if he be their father.
Those Brāhmaṇas who carry out the funeral rites for a Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector partake of the heavenly world.
Having carried out the deceased relative and performed the funeral rites, they should approach the pyre from the left and perform an immersion in water while still wearing their clothes.
Having performed the offering of water for the deceased, they should offer a single funeral ball (piṇḍa) upon kuśa grass.
Having changed their garments, having chewed neem leaves, and having placed their feet upon a stone at the doorway, they should enter the house.
And they should throw unbroken grains into the fire.
On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones.
Their [remains] should be cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
As many years as the number of bones of a person remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that many thousands of years does he dwell in the heavenly world.
As long as the period of impurity lasts, so long should they offer water and a single rice-ball for the deceased.
And they should eat from seats that have been purchased or obtained.
And those who abstain from eating meat.
They should sleep on the bare ground.
And those who sleep separately [from their wives].

Having departed from the village at the end of the period of impurity, and having performed the shaving of their beards, they should enter their homes after bathing with a paste of sesame or mustard seeds, and having changed their garments.
In that case, having performed a propitiatory rite, they should perform the worship of the Brāhmaṇas.
The gods are the invisible gods; the Brāhmaṇas are the visible gods.
The worlds are sustained by the Brāhmaṇas. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 19–21)
By the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, the deities abide in heaven;
the word spoken by a Brāhmaṇa never becomes false anywhere.
Whatever the Brāhmaṇas, being most satisfied, declare, that the deities approve;
when they are satisfied, the deities who are beyond the senses are constantly satisfied in those who are before their eyes.

Those of undaunted spirit should offer consolation to those afflicted by grief for their deceased kin. O Earth, delighter of the mind, I shall now declare to you those words with which they should comfort them.
That which is the northern course of the sun is the day of the gods.
The southern solstice is night.
A year constitutes a day and a night.
Thirty of those [days] constitute a month.
Twelve months constitute a year.
The Kali Yuga consists of twelve hundred divine years.
The Dvāpara [age] has double [the duration of the Tretā].
The Tretā age consists of three times that [duration].
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four times [the duration of the other ages].
Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four yugas.
Seventy-one cycles of the four yugas constitute a manvantara.
And a thousand cycles of the four yugas constitutes a kalpa.
And that [day] is the day of the grandfather (pitāmaha).
And his night is of the same duration.
By calculating months and years through such days and nights, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years.
A day of Puruṣa is delimited by the lifespan of Brahmā.
At the end of that [day], there is a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
That same duration constitutes his night.
There is simply no count of the human days and nights that have already passed.
And [it is not given] for those who are yet to be born.
Because time has no beginning and no end.
Thus, in this supportless time that is constantly moving forward,
I do not perceive any such being whose stability would be permanent.
The grains of sand in the Gaṅgā and the drops of rain when Indra pours down rain may be counted in this world, but the grandfathers (pitāmahas) who have passed away cannot.
In every kalpa, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of mortal men?
And many royal sages, endowed with all virtues,
as well as gods and celestial rishis, have met their death in the course of time.
Those who are capable in this world of being the cause of creation and destruction—
even they are led away by Time, for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Overcome by time, every living being is led to the next world, subject to the snares of their own actions; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no companionship in this world.
Since people here do not benefit the deceased by weeping, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs with both his good deeds and his evil deeds as his companions,
what need has he for kinsmen— whether they grieve or not?
During the period of impurity of his kinsmen, the deceased finds no rest;
therefore, he goes to those very people who offer the funeral cakes and water.
Until the performance of the *sapindīkaraṇa* rite, one who has died remains a *preta*;
to him who has gone to the world of the *pretas*, offer food together with a water-pot.
Having gone to the world of the ancestors, one partakes of food at a śrāddha that is equal to the svadhā offering;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
Whether in the state of a deity, in a place of torment, in the womb of an animal,
or likewise in the human condition, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen.
When the śrāddha has been performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the śrāddha is certain.
Therefore, having abandoned useless grief, the śrāddha should always be performed.
Only this much should always be performed for the deceased by his kinsmen; a man should not grieve, for by grieving he does no service to the deceased nor to himself.
"O men, seeing this world without refuge and your kinsmen dying,
always choose Dharma alone as your companion."
Even a kinsman, though capable, cannot follow a dead man;
for, with the exception of the wife, the path to Yama is closed to everyone else.
"Virtue alone follows him wherever he goes;
indeed, in this worthless world of men, practice virtue without delay."
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what is to be done in the afternoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and carries away one who is attached to fields, shops, or houses, while his mind is elsewhere, just as a she-wolf seizes a lamb.
Time has no one dear to it, nor does it have anyone it hates;
when the lifespan resulting from one's past actions is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings, nor even repeated recitations can save a human being overtaken by death or even by old age.
For even with hundreds of precautions, one is not able to ward off an impending calamity;
what lamentation can there be in that regard?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so too does the fruit of previously performed action certainly find its doer.
Beings are unmanifest at their beginning and manifest in their middle state; then they are indeed unmanifest again at their end. In this regard, what cause for lamentation is there?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age within this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a new garment after discarding one previously worn, so too does the embodied soul take up a new body bound by its past actions.
Weapons do not cut him; fire does not burn him;
water does not moisten him; and the wind does not dry him up.
This [Self] is indeed incapable of being cut, incapable of being burnt, incapable of being moistened, and incapable of being dried;
it is eternal, ever-moving, fixed, immovable, and ancient.
"This [Self] is said to be unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable;
therefore, having understood it thus, you ought not to grieve for it."
Visnu Smṛti 21.1:

Now, at the end of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as he is able, facing northward, and honored with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
One should modify the mantras in the singular when only one person is intended.
In the vicinity of the leavings, he should offer a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) using that person’s name and lineage.

When the Brahmins have finished eating and have been honored with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should offer inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) while pronouncing the name and lineage (gotra) of the deceased, and then dig three furrows—one span (vitasti) long, four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) wide, and as deep as their width—spaced at intervals of that same measure.
Having established three fires near the trenches and having strewn grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each one of them.
To Soma, who is mindful of the ancestors, svadhā! Homage!
To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svadhā! Salutation!
To Yama and Aṅgiras, Svadhā! Homage!
And at the three places, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) as before.
Having filled three trenches with food, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, one should mutter the mantra, "This is for you."
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] on the anniversary of death every month.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, preceded by the deities, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
In this case, one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the offering of water for the feet (pādya).
With the mantra, "May the earth unite with you, and [the waters] that are common," he should pour the water from the *pādya* vessel for the deceased into the three *pādya* vessels for the ancestors.
One should place four rice-balls (piṇḍas) in the vicinity of the leavings.
And having followed the Brāhmaṇas—who have sipped water for purification and received their sacrificial fees—he should dismiss them.
Then, one should place the *preta*-piṇḍa among the three piṇḍas, just like the water from the vessel used for washing the feet.
Even when in close proximity to the three trenches, it is exactly the same.
Having performed the Śrāddha for twelve days according to the procedure for the monthly rites, one should perform the Sapindikarana on the thirteenth day.
For Śūdras, however, [the rite] takes place on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras.
If an intercalary month should occur within the year, then one should increase the period by one day for the purpose of the monthly rite.
The sapindikarana rite for women should be performed in this same manner. Likewise, one should perform the śrāddha for them throughout their lives and every year thereafter.
For one whose *sapindīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for a year.
Visnu Smṛti 22.1: For a Brāhmaṇa, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) upon the birth or death of those with whom he shares the funeral rice-ball (*sapinda*) is ten days.
For a Kṣatriya, it lasts twelve days.
For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days.
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one month.
And the sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person.
During a period of impurity, the performance of fire-oblations, giving, receiving gifts, and the private recitation of the Veda are suspended.
One should not eat the food of anyone while they are in a state of impurity.
If one eats food even once during the period of impurity of Brāhmaṇas and others, his own period of impurity lasts as long as theirs.
Upon the cessation of the period of impurity, one should perform the penance.

If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a person of his own caste, he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, mutter the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
But during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by fasting and performing this very same rite.
And a Kṣatriya [is subject to impurity] during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya.
During the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.

During the period of impurity caused by the death of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the period of impurity caused by the death of a Vaiśya, one should go to a flowing river and mutter the Gāyatrī five hundred times.
And a Vaiśya, during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, shall mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a Śūdra should perform a ritual bath during the period of impurity of the twice-born.
A Śūdra, having bathed during the period of impurity caused by another Śūdra, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master, provided they follow the natural order of castes.
When the master has died, [the property] belongs to oneself.
In the case of those of lower caste [having intercourse] with sapindas of higher caste, purification occurs at the end of that [latter's] period of impurity.
For a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of sapinda relations who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods of impurity are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively.
For a Kṣatriya [committing adultery] with a Vaiśya or a Śūdra woman, the penance lasts six nights or three nights respectively.
For a Vaiśya among Śūdras, [the purification] occurs after six nights.
In the case of a miscarriage, the penance lasts for as many days and nights as there were months of gestation.
If a child is born dead, or if it dies immediately after birth, there is immediate purification for the family.
When a child who has not yet cut its teeth dies, the purification occurs immediately.
For him there is neither the rite of cremation with fire nor the offering of water.
But when teeth have appeared, yet before the tonsure ceremony has been performed, purification occurs after one day and night.
But if the tonsure ceremony has been performed but the other rites have not yet been completed, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
After that, according to the time as previously prescribed.
For women, marriage is the purificatory rite (saṃskāra).
In the case of women who have been consecrated through marriage, there is no impurity on the paternal side.
If her birth or death should occur while she is in her father’s house, then there shall be one night and three nights [of impurity] respectively.
If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of a birth-impurity, then purification occurs upon the conclusion of the first impurity.
If it remains until the end of the night, [the purification is] by two days.
In the morning, [the purification occurs] in three days.
During the period of impurity caused by a death, if another death occurs among one's kinsmen, the same rule applies.
Having heard of births or deaths while residing in another country, one shall become pure by means of the remainder of the period of impurity.
When the period of impurity has passed, [the purification] at the end of a year is achieved by means of a single night.
After that, [he becomes pure] by means of bathing.
When the preceptor and the maternal grandfather have passed away, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
When sons other than the legitimate son of the body have been born or have died;
and when wives who had previously been with another man have given birth or have died.

If the wife or son of one's teacher (ācārya), a sub-teacher (upādhyāya), a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, or a fellow student or pupil has died, purification occurs after one night.
And also toward the king of one's own country.
And when a person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* has died in one's own house.
There is no period of impurity for those killed by Bhṛgu (a falling star), fire, fasting, water, in battle, by lightning, or by the king.
Nor [is it an offense] for kings in the performance of their royal duties.
Nor [should one eat] during the vow of those observing a religious vow.
Nor [should one study] during the sacrificial session of those performing a *sattra* sacrifice.
Nor [is it forbidden] for artisans when performing the work of an artisan.
Nor for those who carry out the king's orders, provided it is by his own will.
Nor [is there a prohibition] regarding the installation of a deity or a marriage, provided the necessary materials have been previously collected.
Nor when there is confusion regarding the country.
Even in times of distress, one must not [act] in such a way as to cause suffering.
Those who commit suicide and those who are outcasts do not partake in the impurity rites or the water libations.
On the death-day of one who has fallen [from his caste], a female slave should cast away a jar of water with her foot.
He who cuts the rope of one who has died by hanging is purified by the Tapta-kṛcchra penance.
And the one who performs the funeral rites for those who have committed suicide.
And one who causes the shedding of those tears [is also liable].
For every deceased person, [the purification] occurs through bathing after the relatives have shed tears together.
If the collection of bones has not yet been performed, purification occurs by bathing with one's clothes on.

A twice-born man, having followed the funeral procession of a Śūdra, shall go to a river, immerse himself in it, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
For the funeral rites of a deceased twice-born man, [the recitation] is one hundred and eight [times].
A Śūdra, having followed a deceased person, shall perform a ritual bath.
Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all social classes (varṇas) should perform a ritual bath.
In the case of sexual intercourse, a bad dream, blood in the throat, and after vomiting or purging; ViṣṇuSm 22.67.
And also when the shaving of the beard has been performed.
And having touched one who has touched a corpse, as well as a menstruating woman, a Caṇḍāla, or the remains of a sacrificial post (yūpa).
One should avoid the flesh of five-toed animals—excluding those that are edible—as well as their bones and fat.
In all these baths, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
A woman in her menses becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Having touched a menstruating woman of a lower caste, a menstruating woman herself shall not eat until she has become purified.
Having touched a woman of his own caste or one of a higher caste, he becomes pure immediately after bathing.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or being desirous of eating or studying; having drunk, bathed, spat, put on a garment, walked upon a road, voided urine or feces, or touched the bone of a five-toed animal that is not fatty—one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
And also upon conversing with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha.
If one is defiled below the navel or on the forearms by bodily impurities, by spirituous liquors, or by intoxicants, one becomes pure by washing that limb with earth and water.
If he is struck elsewhere, he becomes pure by washing that specific limb with earth and water and then bathing.
But one whose food has been defiled by the mouth [of another] should fast and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And one whose lip has been struck by a tooth [is also unfit].
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nails,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Gauḍī, mādhvī, and paiṣṭī are to be known as the three kinds of liquor (surā).
Just as one is, so are all; they must not be drunk by the twice-born.
The juice of madhūka, that of sugarcane, ṭāṅka, kaula, dates, and breadfruit; the juice of grapes, honey-wine (mādhvīka), maireya, and that which is produced from coconuts.
These ten intoxicating drinks are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them.
But a disciple who performs the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛmedha) for his deceased guru becomes purified there by ten nights together with those who consume the funeral offerings (pretāhāra).
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, a sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has died, one who is under a vow is not deprived of his vow.

One who has been assigned a penance shall not perform the water-libation rite until the completion of that vow; but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after exactly three nights.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water,
collyrium, wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Of all forms of purity, the purity of food is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure regarding food is truly pure, not he who is merely purified by earth and water.
The learned are purified by forbearance; those who have committed improper acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers; and those most proficient in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This determination regarding bodily purification has been declared to you;
now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by spirituous liquors, or by fermented intoxicants is considered "extremely defiled."
Every iron vessel that has been excessively defiled is purified by being cast into fire.
An object made of gemstone or stone, as well as a lotus, is purified by burying it in the earth for seven nights.
[One should avoid] that which consists of horn, ivory, or bone, by means of carving.
One should discard a vessel made of wood or one made of clay.
If a garment that has been excessively defiled becomes clean only after being washed, one should cut it away.
Objects made of gold, silver, lotus, or gems are purified by water alone, provided they are free from stains.
[The purification] of stone vessels, chalices, and cups.
The *caru* vessel, the *sruk*, and the *sruva* ladles [should be cleansed] with hot water.
In the performance of a sacrifice, by wiping the sacrificial vessels with the hand.
The sacrificial wooden sword (sphya), winnowing basket (śūrpa), cart (śakaṭa), pestle (musala), and mortar (ulūkhala) are purified by sprinkling water over them.
And also of beds, vehicles, and seats. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 23.12)
And [the same applies] when there are many [offenders].
And [the same applies] to grain, skins, ropes, woven goods, articles made of split bamboo, threads, and cotton cloth.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers.
And likewise for grass, wood, and dry leaves.
By washing these [vessels]. Visnusmṛti 23.17.
And also for small quantities.
Silk and woolen cloth are purified with alkaline salts.
With *ariṣṭaka* wood for the *kutapa* vessels.
[The purification] of silk cloths is by means of *śrīphala* fruits.
[The purification] of linen garments is with white mustard seeds.
And [the same applies] to objects made of horn, bone, and ivory.
[The purification] of skins from deer hair is by means of lotus seeds.
Objects made of copper, brass, tin, and lead [are purified] with acidic water.
One should purify bell-metal and iron with ashes.
By carving wood. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 23.27)
[The purification] of things produced from fruit is by means of cow-hair [brushes].
For solid objects, purification is by sprinkling; thus says Viṣṇu Smṛti 23.29.
The purification of liquids is by means of straining.
In the case of large quantities of molasses and other products of sugarcane stored in the house, [the penance is] by extinguishing them with water or fire.
And [the same applies] to all types of salt. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 23.32)
For earthen vessels, purification is by means of re-firing.
For images of deities that have been purified like material objects, [the expiation is] by means of re-consecration.
If food that has not yet been prepared is defiled, one should discard only that portion which was defiled; for the remainder, one should perform threshing and washing.
Food prepared in an amount exceeding one *droṇa* is not defiled even if it has been touched by an impurity.
Having merely removed that which has been defiled from it, one should pour gold-infused water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra into it, and one should show it to a goat and to fire.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
In all purifications of objects, earth and water should be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from that which has been smeared by it.
A goat and a horse are pure in their mouths; neither a cow nor human excrement is impure [in those locations]. Roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun, and by the wind.
Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows,
as well as structures built of baked bricks, are purified by the wind alone.
Furthermore, for all living beings, one should effect purification with earth and water;
and for those who are extremely defiled, purification must always be performed without negligence.
Water on the ground is meritorious where it satisfies the thirst of a cow;
likewise is water situated on a stone, provided it is not contaminated by impurities.
From a well containing a dead five-clawed animal, or one that is otherwise utterly defiled,
one should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth.

One should perform the kindling of the fire in a well that has been lined with baked bricks; subsequently, one should pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a well newly filled with water.
O Earth, in the case of small and stagnant reservoirs of water, purification is declared to be like that for a well; however, there is no fault in large ones.
The gods ordained three things as pure for Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
so too is almsfood received through a Brāhmaṇa intermediary, and all mines.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing a deer.
The flesh of one killed by dogs is declared to be pure;
so too is that of one killed by carnivorous beasts, or by others such as Caṇḍālas and robbers.
One should designate as pure those apertures of the body that are above the navel;
those below are impure, as are the excretions discharged from the body.
Flies, droplets, shadows, a cow, an elephant, a horse,
sunbeams, dust, the earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The primary drops that fall upon the limbs do not make one impure by being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa);
nor do those which enter the mouth as beard hairs, nor what is caught between the teeth.
The drops that touch the feet of one who is making others sip water for purification should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
But if one who has something in his hand is somehow touched by leavings,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without setting that object down.
A house is purified by sweeping and smearing; a book, by sprinkling;
and [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping.
The purification of the ground is achieved by burning it, or else by the dwelling of cows upon it. Cows are purifying and auspicious; in cows, all the worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all sins.
Cow's urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and yellow pigment (rocanā)—[these are the products of the cow].
This supreme water from the horns of cows is the most auspicious of all things; it is sacred and the destroyer of every sin.
Scratching the bodies of cows is the destroyer of all sins;
by giving morsels of food to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows, and nourishment is increased in their dust;
Lakṣmī resides in their dried dung, and Dharma in bowing to them; therefore, one should constantly perform prostration to them.
VisnuSm 24.1: Now, for a Brāhmaṇa, there are four wives according to the sequence of the castes.
For a Kṣatriya, there are three.
For a Vaiśya, there are two.
For a Śūdra, there is one [tooth-stick].
In the case of marrying one of these women who is of the same caste (savarṇā), the hand should be taken in marriage.
In the case of marrying a girl of a different caste, a Kṣatriya girl incurs a Śara penance.
A goad [is the token] for the daughter of a Vaiśya.
[The marriage] with a Śūdra girl [is performed] within the hem of the garment.
One should not take as a wife a woman who belongs to the same *gotra* or who shares the same *ārṣa-pravara*.
On the mother's side up to the fifth generation, and on the father's side up to the seventh generation; nor one who is not of noble birth.
Nor one who is diseased.
Nor one with an extra limb.
Nor one who has a deficient limb.
Nor one that is excessively tawny.
Nor one who is talkative.
Now, there are eight forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca [are the eight forms of marriage].
Having invited a man of virtuous qualities, the giving away of a daughter is the Brāhma marriage.
The gift given to a priest officiating at a sacrifice is called *daiva*.
By the mention of "a pair of cows," the Ārṣa form of marriage is indicated.
By giving what has been requested, the Prājāpatya rite is accomplished.
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two people who desire each other, occurring in the absence of their mother and father.
Through purchase, it is the Āsura form.
The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] occurs by carrying off [the bride] during battle.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 24.26: From approaching [a woman] while she is asleep or intoxicated, the Paiśāca rite arises.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 24.27: Among these, the first four are lawful.
The Gāndharva form of marriage is also permitted for Kṣatriyas.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman purifies twenty-one generations of men.
The son of a Daiva marriage is the fourteenth.
And the son of an Ārṣī wife is the seventh.
The Prājāpatya penance consists of four [days].
By giving away a daughter in the Brāhma form of marriage, one causes her to go to the world of Brahmā.
By means of the Daiva rite, one attains heaven.
The Vaiṣṇava [rite] is performed according to the Ārṣa [method].
By the Prājāpatya penance, one attains the world of the gods.
Through the Gāndharva rite, one goes to the world of the Gandharvas.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, the maternal grandfather, and the mother—these are the givers of a maiden in marriage.
In the absence of the preceding one, each subsequent person, remaining in his natural state, [is the next in order].
A maiden, having waited through three menstrual seasons, may choose a husband for herself;
but once three seasons have passed, she always has the power over her own self.
A maiden who, while still in her father’s house and before being consecrated by marriage, sees her menses, is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; he who takes her does not incur guilt.
VisnuSm 25:
Now, the duties of women.
She must practice the same vows as her husband.
Worship of one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, teacher, deity, and guest.
The state of having well-refined implements.
Not having open hands [when giving].
The state of having well-concealed vessels.
A lack of interest in the fundamental rites.
Devotion to auspicious conduct and its observance.
When the husband has gone abroad, she shall not perform acts of personal adornment.
One should not enter the houses of others.
One must not remain standing near the doorway, the water-trough for cattle, or the axle of a cart.
In all ritual acts, there is a lack of independence.
In childhood, youth, and old age alike, there is dependence upon the father, the husband, and the son.
When her husband has died, she shall observe lifelong celibacy or ascend the funeral pyre after him.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even fasting;
by that which she performs in service to her husband, she is glorified in heaven.
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living,
she takes away his life-span and goes to hell.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those lifelong students of the Veda.

When there are several wives of the same caste, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest. However, when they are of mixed castes, he may do so even with the youngest, provided she is of the same caste as himself.
In the absence of a woman of the same caste, however, he may marry one of the next lower caste even in times of distress.
But a twice-born man must never [beget a son] with a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra wife for a twice-born man can never serve the purpose of dharma;
she is declared to be for his pleasure alone, for he is blinded by passion.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry a woman of a lower caste,
quickly bring their own families, along with their progeny, down to the status of Śūdras.
But for him whose rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests have those [impure persons] as their primary agents,
neither the ancestors nor the gods eat, and he does not go to heaven.
VisnuSm 27.01: When the pregnancy becomes clearly manifest, the rite of impregnation (niṣeka) is performed.
The *puṃsavana* rite is to be performed before the fetus begins to move.
In the sixth or eighth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed;
and when a son is born, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed.
Upon the cessation of the period of impurity, the naming ceremony (nāmadheya) is performed.
Auspicious [ornaments] are for the Brāhmaṇa.
For a Kṣatriya, [the punishment] is more severe.
That which is accompanied by wealth belongs to the Vaiśya.
That which is contemptible belongs to the Śūdra.
In the fourth month, there is the beholding of the sun.
In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed.
These very same rites for women are performed without mantras.
Their marriage is accompanied by mantras.
The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh month from conception, [the initiation] of a king [is performed].
In the twelfth month from conception, the Viśas [attain the status of twice-born].
For them, the girdles made of muñja grass, bowstring, and balbaja grass are [the prescribed] muñjī-girdles.
The sacred threads and garments may be made of cotton, hemp, or wool.
The skins of the black antelope, the tiger, and the goat.
The staffs are made of palāśa, khadira, or udumbara wood.
The [lengths of the staffs] are equal to the tips of the hair, the forehead, and the region of the nose, respectively.
Or all [of them] together.
They should be straight and possessed of their bark.
One should wander for alms beginning with the word "bhavat," using the word "bhavat" in the middle, and ending with the word "bhavat."
The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year,
nor for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, nor for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this time, if these three also remain uninitiated according to the prescribed period,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vrātyas, and are censured by the noble.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle are prescribed for him, whatever staff and whatever garment [are prescribed], those same shall be used by him even during his religious observances (vratas).
Having cast away into the water his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread, and water-pot when they are worn out, he should take others while reciting the mantras.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 28:
Now follows the residence of religious students (brahmacārins) in the teacher's household.
The worship of the two twilights (saṃdhyā).
One should recite the morning twilight prayer while standing, and the evening twilight prayer while seated.
At two times of the day, he should perform the rites of ritual bathing and tending the sacred fire.
In water, one shall perform an immersion like that of a staff.
Visnu Smṛti 28.6: Studying when summoned.
One should practice what is pleasing and beneficial to the teacher.
Wearing the girdle, the staff, the deerskin, and the sacred thread.
Except for the household of his teacher, he should go about begging alms from those who possess virtuous qualities.
The consumption of almsfood authorized by the guru.

One should avoid salt, fermented gruel (*śukta*), stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, the remnants of others' meals, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech during the performance of a *śrāddha*.
He shall sleep on the ground.
One should rise before one's teacher and go to bed after him.
Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), he should perform the salutation of the guru.
And with his hands crossed, he should touch his feet.
The right [hand] with the right [hand], and the other [hand] with the other [hand].
And at the conclusion of the salutation, he should announce his own name, ending with the word "bhoḥ."
Whether standing, sitting, lying down, eating, or facing away, one should not address him.

One standing should serve one who is seated; one walking toward him should serve one who is walking; one approaching should go out to meet one who is coming; and one running should follow behind one who is running.
Facing one who has turned his face away.
Having approached the presence of one who is standing at a distance.
Having prostrated before one who is lying down.
And while within his range of vision, one should not sit at will.
And one should not utter his name alone.
One should not imitate his gait, gestures, speech, and so forth.
Wherever there may be censure or slander of him, he should not remain there.
He should not share a single seat with him.
Except for [riding] on stone, wooden planks, or boats.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as one would toward one's own teacher.
And one who has not been instructed by his teacher should not salute his own elders.
One should behave toward a teacher’s son who is younger, of equal age, or an instructor, as one would toward the teacher himself.
One should not wash his feet.
One should not eat what is left over as leavings.
In this manner, one should acquire one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas.

But he who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, goes to the state of a Śūdra along with his progeny.
The first birth is from the mother; the second is the tying of the girdle (mauñjī-bandhana).
In this regard, for him the Sāvitrī is his mother, while the teacher (ācārya) is his father. By this very fact, they possess the status of the twice-born.
Before the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, a twice-born man is equal to a Śūdra.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should remain either shaven-headed or with matted hair.
After completing the acquisition of the Veda, having been permitted by his teacher and having given him a gift, he should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna).
Then, he should spend the remainder of his life in the teacher’s family or in the forest from the time of birth.
In that case, when the teacher has died, one should behave toward the teacher’s son as one would toward the teacher himself.
[The same penance applies] for [intercourse] with the wives of one's teacher or with women of the same caste.
In the absence of that, he should become a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī) intent on the service of the sacred fires.
The Brahmin who thus practices celibacy without sloth goes to the highest station and is not born here again.
The intentional emission of semen by a twice-born man who is observing a vow.
Those who know the Dharma say that for a religious student (brahmacārin), there is a transgression of his vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having donned the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses while proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them and eating only once a day, and performing ablutions three times a day, he becomes purified after one year.
If a twice-born student (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
If, while not being ill, one fails to go for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for an *avakīrṇin*.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
But he who, having performed the initiation and the instruction in the vows, should teach the Veda, one should know him as the Ācārya.
But he who teaches this for a fee is an *upādhyāya*, or [one who teaches] a single portion.
One should know that he who performs another's sacrificial rites is his officiating priest (ṛtvij).
One should not employ anyone who has not been tested.
One should not teach [the Veda].
One should not initiate him [into the sacred thread].
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two perishes or incurs enmity.
Where neither virtue nor wealth exists, nor even a corresponding degree of service,
there knowledge must not be imparted, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
"Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: 'Protect me; I am your treasure.'"
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, dishonest, or lacking self-restraint; in that way, I shall remain full of power.

Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the Vedic hymns on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, one should study for four and a half months.
Then he should perform their dismissal outside.
Between the rites of Utsarjana and Upākarma, one should engage in the study of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas).
One should not study for a day and a night on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
Nor during the impurity caused by the commencement of another season or by an eclipse.
Nor during the departure of Indra.
Nor when a violent wind is blowing.
Nor [should one study] during unseasonable rain, lightning, or thunder.
Nor during earthquakes, the falling of meteors, or the flaming of the quarters of the sky.
Nor in a village where a funeral ceremony is being performed.
Nor when there is a conflict between scriptural authorities.
Nor when there is the howling of dogs, jackals, or donkeys.

Nor one who has vomited.

By studying that [text], there is a loss of life for both the teacher and the pupil.

One should understand that the "origination" (saṃbhūti) of this person— which occurs when he is born here from a womb— is that which his mother and father produce together through mutual desire.
The caste that the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that caste is real, undecaying, and immortal.

VisnuSm 31:
There are three who are exceedingly venerable to a man.
The mother, the father, and the teacher.
One must always be intent on serving them.
Whatever they may tell him, that he should do.
One should act for their pleasure and welfare.
Without their permission, one should not do anything at all.

The mother’s sister, the father’s sister, and the elder sister.

Setting in motion a great machine.
The injury of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and medicinal herbs.
The livelihood of a woman [is as follows]. VisnuSm 37-25.
And there is engagement in acts of sorcery and rites for the sake of power.
The undertaking of ritual actions for one's own sake.
Not maintaining the sacred fires.
The non-discharge of debts owed to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
VisnuSm 37.30: Studying false scriptures.
Atheism (VisnuSm 37.31).
[One becomes] like a bard (kuśīlava). *Viṣṇusmṛti* 37.32.
Drinking liquor and consorting with women [unfit for intercourse].
Thus end the minor offenses (upapātakas), Viṣṇu Smṛti 37.34.

Deceit.

or else, the Kṛcchra-Atikṛcchra is the purifying expiation.

Those who have committed heinous sins (atipātakin) and have not performed expiation for these shall be cooked in turn for a kalpa.
Those who have committed mortal sins [remain so] for the duration of a Manvantara.
And those who have committed secondary sins (anupātakin).
Those who have committed minor offenses [must wait] for four yugas.
And those who have committed the act of causing mixture of castes [must remain outside] for a thousand years.
And those who have committed acts causing loss of caste.
And those who have committed acts that cause loss of caste (apātrīkaraṇa).
And those who have committed acts that cause impurity.
And those who have committed miscellaneous sins [shall remain so] for many series of years.
Sinful men who have committed offenses, immediately after giving up their lives,
reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Just as they are dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama, being led along with great difficulty and groaning.
Being devoured by dogs, jackals, and flesh-eaters such as crows, herons, and cranes,
as well as by fire-mouthed beings, serpents, and scorpions.
Being burned by fire, pierced by thorns,
split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst;
Tormented by hunger and likewise by fierce packs of tigers,
they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others,
they are beaten by servants with faces resembling those of terrifying crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and in some places they are crushed against iron and stone slabs.
In some places they eat vomit, and in others pus and blood;
in some places excrement, and in others flesh that has the foul odor of pus—most dreadful indeed.
They remain in dreadful darknesses, and in some places they are being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like beaks.
In some places they are afflicted by cold, and in others they dwell amidst impurities;
furthermore, in some places those most dreadful ghosts devour one another.
In some places they are struck by spirits; likewise, in some places they are suspended;
in some places they are hurled by showers of arrows, and in others they are cut to pieces.
With their feet placed upon thorns and entwined by the coils of serpents,
they are likewise tormented by mechanical devices and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, with needle-like throats, and most dreadful,
they possess bodies as large as mountain peaks, yet are capable of enduring only torment.
Thus, having experienced their sin as suffering beings, those who have committed offenses enter into animal wombs and endure various miseries.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 44:
Now, for those of sinful nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there arise births in the wombs of animals.
For those who have committed the most heinous crimes (atipātakin), there is a succession through all the immobile wombs (sthāvara-yoni).
And those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter the wombs of worms.
Those who have committed minor offenses (anupātakin) are born into the wombs of birds.
For those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), there are births from aquatic sources.
For those who have committed acts that cause loss of caste, there are births in the wombs of aquatic creatures.
Those who have committed acts that cause the confusion of castes enter the wombs of animals.
Those who have committed acts that cause loss of caste (apātrīkaraṇa) are born as animals.
Among humans, those who have committed acts that cause impurity (malinīkaraṇa) are born into castes that are untouchable.
Regarding miscellaneous offenses, those who commit miscellaneous acts indeed become predatory carnivorous creatures.
One who eats food that is unfit to be eaten or consumed becomes a worm.
A thief becomes a hawk.
A snake is one that steals the excellent path.
A mouse that steals grain [is the expiation].
A swan is he who steals bell-metal.
One who carries water [in a vessel] and one who bathes repeatedly in water.
The honey-bee. VisnuSm 44-17.
Milk is for the crow.
He should taste [it] with his tongue.
A mongoose [destroys] the clarified butter.
One who eats meat becomes a vulture.

A lizard [is the expiation] for a cow.

A muskrat [is purified] by perfumes.
A leaf-vegetable is [the gift] for Barhiṣad.

Household implements for domestic work.

One who suffers from leprosy is an atipātakin (one who has committed a most heinous sin).
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with consumption.
A drinker of *surā* shall have black teeth.

But one who steals food becomes afflicted with chronic disease.
One who steals speech becomes mute.
One who steals clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo.
One who steals a horse becomes lame.
One who reviles the gods or Brahmins becomes mute.
One with a flickering tongue is a poisoner.
One who is insane and one who sets fire [to another's property] are [excluded from inheritance].
One who is hostile toward his guru becomes afflicted with epilepsy.
But the killer of a cow becomes blind.
And one who steals a lamp.
One who is one-eyed and one who extinguishes lamps [are both excluded].
A washerman is one who sells tin, chowries, and lead.
A seller of single-hoofed animals becomes a hunter of wild beasts.
One who eats from a sacrificial pit has a mutilated mouth.
A bell-ringer is a thief.
A usurer is a "bee-like" person (bhrāmarī).
One who has cleansed his mouth becomes solitary and suffers from abdominal tumors caused by wind.
One who breaks an agreement becomes a bald-headed man.
One who has had sexual intercourse with a woman of low caste becomes an *avakīrṇin*.
One who destroys the livelihood of others becomes poor.
One who causes pain to others becomes afflicted with a chronic disease.
Thus, according to their specific actions, they are born endowed with particular marks:
afflicted by disease, or likewise blind, hunchbacked, lame, or one-eyed.
Dwarfs, the deaf, the mute, the weak, and others as well—
therefore, one should perform expiation with every possible effort.
Now follow the *kṛcchra* penances.
He shall not eat for three days.
And he should perform his bath three times every day—at dawn, noon, and sunset.
At each bath, one should immerse oneself in the water three times.
Submerged [in water], one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Standing during the day, he should remain standing.
At night, he shall remain seated.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
Thus ends the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
One should eat in the evening for three days, in the morning for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days; this is the Prājāpatya penance.
For three days one should drink hot water, for three days hot ghee, for three days hot milk, and for three days one should not eat at all; this is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
The *śītakṛcchra* consists of these same [substances] when they are cold.
The *atikṛcchra* penance consists of subsisting on milk alone for twenty-one days.
The Udakakṛcchra penance consists of consuming water and barley-meal for one month.
By consuming lotus stalks, one performs the Mūla-kṛcchra penance.
The Śrīphala-kṛcchra consists of subsisting on bilva fruits.
Or with lotus-seeds.
For one who abstains from food, the Parāka penance is completed in twelve days.
One should consume cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass for one day, and fast on the second day. This is the *sāṃtapana* penance.
The Mahāsāntapana penance consists of the daily practice of consuming cow urine and the other [five substances].
And by practicing [the consumption of] these for three days, one performs the Atisāntapana penance.
The consumption of oil-cake, rice-scum, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, with an interval of fasting between each, constitutes the Tulāpuruṣa penance.
The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of each of the following: *kuśa*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vaṭa*, *brāhmī*, and *suvarcalā*.
One who has undergone the tonsure should perform all these Kṛcchra penances,
bathing daily at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and having his senses subdued.
One should avoid excessive conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts; one should constantly recite purificatory prayers and offer oblations according to one's ability.
VisnuSm 47:
Now, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should eat mouthfuls that have not been altered.

One should increase those [meals] during the waxing of the moon's digit and decrease them during its waning; on the new moon day, one should not eat. This is the Cāndrāyaṇa penance known as "middle like a barley grain" (yavamadhyacāndrāyaṇa).
Or it may be "middle-sized like an ant."
That [lunar month] in which the new moon occurs during the middle [of the fortnight] is called "ant-like in the middle" (pipīlikā-madhya).
That for which the full moon occurs [at the junction of the two halves] is the *yavamadhyama* (barley-shaped).
If one eats eight morsels every day for a month, that is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*.
Eating four morsels each at evening and four at morning constitutes the *saśiśu-cāndrāyaṇa*.
If one eats in any manner whatsoever thirty meals less sixty during a month, that is the Sāmānya-Cāndrāyaṇa.
O Earth, in ancient times, having performed this vow, the stainless Seven Sages,
as well as Brahmā and Rudra, attained the supreme abode.
VisnuSm 48.1:
Now, if one should consider oneself heavy with the weight of actions committed by oneself, one should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for one's own sake.
One should not offer oblations into the fire from that [vessel].
And in this case, there is no rite of offering (bali-karma).
One should consecrate with mantras the food that is uncooked, that which is being cooked, and that which has been cooked.
While it is being cooked, one should perform the ritual protection.
Brahmā among the gods, the path of the poets, the seer among the learned, the buffalo among wild beasts,
the hawk among vultures, the axe among the forests— Soma, chanting, transcends the filter.
Thus he binds the darbha grass.
And one should eat that boiled rice after pouring it into a vessel.

"Those gods who are born of the mind, who delight in the mind, who are highly skillful, and whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us; may they favor us; obeisance to them! Svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer the oblation into oneself.
Then, having finished rinsing his mouth, he should touch his navel.

"O Waters, having been bathed in you, may you become drinkable; O Yavas, dwell within our bellies. May they be for us free from disease, free from consumption, and free from sin—divine, immortal, and increasers of Truth. Thus [he says].
One who desires virility [should observe] a fast for three nights.
One who commits a sin [is purified] after six nights.
Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins (mahāpātaka).
By twelve nights [of fasting], one burns away even the sin committed by one's ancestors.
Having drunk [it] for a month, all sins [are destroyed].
And for those who have been released from being carried off by cattle, [the penance lasts] twenty-one nights of barley.
"You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey. You are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier held sacred by the seers."
Ghee is barley, honey is barley, and water is barley— the immortal barley—
may all of them purify whatever sin or any evil deed I have committed.
O barley grains, destroy for me misfortune and Kālakarṇī— the evil deed committed by speech, the action performed by hand, and the ill-thought thought conceived by the mind.
O Yavas, purify for me that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, that which is defiled by the remains of food,
and the failure to serve my mother and father.
The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a birth-impurity,
the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral— purify these for me with barley.
The child-deceiver, the unrighteous man, and whatever is done at the king’s gate;
the theft of gold, the vrātya-status, and the officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice; the reviling of brahmins—purify these, O my barley grains!
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva on the twelfth day.
With flowers, incense, unguents, lamps, and food offerings, and by the satiation of the fire and the Brahmins.
Having performed this vow for one year, one becomes purified from sins.
Having performed this throughout one's life, one attains Śvetadvīpa.
By performing this on the twelfth days of both fortnights for one year, one attains the heavenly world.
Having performed it throughout one's life, [one attains] the world of Viṣṇu.
In this very same way, it is also [to be performed] on the fifteenth days.
By attending upon Keśava as the embodiment of Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day,
and as the embodiment of Yoga, one shall attain the Great.
When the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky on a full-moon day,
that specific full-moon day within the year is declared to be "Mahatī" (the Great).
On that day, acts such as giving gifts and fasting are proclaimed to yield inexhaustible merit.
Likewise, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight which is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism [is similarly meritorious].
Having constructed a hut of leaves in the forest, he should dwell there.
He should bathe at the three daily sessions.
Proclaiming his own deed, he should practice begging for alms from village to village.
And he should sleep on a bed of grass.
This is the Great Vow (mahāvrata).
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one shall perform [the penance] for twelve years.
A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice.
Nor one who is pregnant or menstruating.
Or a woman of the Atri lineage.
Or a friend. VisnuSm 50.10.
In the case of killing a king, one should perform the Mahāvrata penance itself for double the duration.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, the penance is one-quarter less.
In the case of killing a Vaiśya, the penance is half [of that prescribed for a Kṣatriya].
Half of that [penance] is for killing a Śūdra.
In all [these cases], he shall have a corpse's head as his banner.
For one month, having undergone a shave, he should follow after cows.
While they are seated, he should remain seated.
And he should remain standing when [the others] are standing.
And he should rescue those who are sinking.
And he should protect [them] from fears.
Without having provided them protection against cold and other such elements, one should not provide it for oneself.
One should bathe with cow urine.
And he should subsist on cow-products.
One should perform this cow-vow in the event of killing a cow.
Having killed an elephant, one should give five dark-blue bulls as a gift.
A horse or a garment.
For killing a donkey, one should give a one-year-old ox.
And for the killing of a ram or a goat.
In the case of killing a camel, the penance is one *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala*.
Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a water-snake, or a python, one should fast, feed a Brahmin with *kṛsara* (rice and peas), and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee.
Upon killing a monitor lizard, an owl, a crow, or a fish, one shall fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of these—a swan, a crane, a balākā, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a ruddy goose—one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a spade made of black iron.
Having killed a eunuch, one [should perform penance for] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, one [should give] a jar of clarified butter.
For killing a partridge, one [must give] a drona of sesame seeds.
A parrot that is two years old, like a calf.
A three-year-old krauñca bird [is the sacrificial fee].
Upon killing a carnivorous beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a carnivorous wild animal, [one should give] a heifer.
For killing an animal not specifically mentioned, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he should give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should fast.
But for the killing of a thousand creatures possessing bones,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
But for killing animals with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited as a prayer;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food,
those born from fluids, and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛta) is the means of purification.
For the unauthorized taking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
A drinker of *surā* is excluded from all ritual acts and shall eat only grains for a year.
Upon consuming any one of the impure substances or intoxicants, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And [the same penance applies] for eating garlic, onions, leeks, things having their smell, village pigs, village cocks, monkeys, or the flesh of cows.
In all these cases for the twice-born, at the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the sacramental rite once again.
In the rite of re-consecration (punar-saṃskāra), shaving the head, wearing a girdle, carrying a staff, and the practice of begging for alms—these vows must be avoided.
If one eats the meat of five-toed animals, excluding the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one shall fast for seven nights.
Having eaten the food of a group, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights.
The food of a carpenter and that of a leather-worker [are forbidden].
And [the food] of usurers, misers, those initiated for a sacrifice, those bound in fetters, those accused of crimes, and eunuchs.
And [the food] of a eunuch, a hypocrite, a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, a fierce person, and one who eats the remnants of another's meal.
And [the food] of a woman whose husband is missing, of a goldsmith, of one whose husband has a rival wife, and of those who have fallen from their caste.
And [the same applies] for those who are slanderers, speakers of falsehood, those who have violated their dharma, and those who sell their own vital essence.
And [the food] of actors, weavers, ungrateful persons, and washermen [is forbidden].
And [the same applies] to those who work with leather, Niṣādas, actors, wrestlers, fletchers, and sellers of weapons.
And [the food] of one who lives by his own [craft], a vintner, an oil-presser, a weaver, and a washerman.
And [the same applies] to those who have sexual intercourse with a menstruating woman, with an adulterer, or with a woman of the lowest caste.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow [is unfit for consumption].
That which has been intentionally touched with the foot or sneezed upon; VisnuSm 51.18.
And [the evidence] of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease [is not admissible].
Meat that has not been honored and meat offered in vain.
Except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohitaka*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* fish, one should fast for three nights upon eating the flesh of any other fish.
And for eating the flesh of any aquatic creature.
Having drunk water kept in a vessel that once held liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those who have stayed in a vessel that held liquor [become pure] after five nights.
A drinker of Soma who smells the breath of a drinker of Surā, having immersed himself in water and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra three times, should perform the consumption of clarified butter.
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten unknown meat, or dried meat from a slaughterhouse.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals or birds, one shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If one eats the flesh of the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, haṃsa, rajjudāla, sārasa, dātyūha, śuka, sārikā, baka, balākā, kokila, or khañjarīṭa, one shall fast for three nights.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of one-hoofed animals and those with two rows of teeth.
And for eating the meat of any bird, with the exception of the partridge, the grey partridge, the quail, the francolin, and the peacock, one must fast for a day and a night.
If one eats insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā* for one day.
And [the same penance applies] for eating the flesh of dogs.
For eating mushrooms or fungi, one must perform the Sāntapana penance.
Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, or milk, as well as oily substances, fermented acids, and *khāṇḍava*, one should fast after consuming whatever food has become stale.
One should avoid juices from trees that grow from cuttings or from impure sources, as well as those that are red.
The lotus-root, meat cooked without ritual purpose, kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, fried cakes, food offered to the gods, and sacrificial oblations—these are forbidden.
