And all milks, with the exception of those from cows, goats, and buffaloes.
Even those [days] do not extend beyond ten days.
And the milk of a cow that is dripping [milk], one in heat, or one whose calf is absent.
And those who eat impure food.
And fermented liquids (śukta) alone, with the exception of curd.
A student in the stage of celibacy (brahmacārin) who eats at a śrāddha feast shall fast for three nights.
And he should dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, the Prājāpatya penance is prescribed.
In the case of eating the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
If one eats the leavings of one's own food, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
For eating the excrement or urine of five-toed animals, one must observe a penance for seven nights.
If one eats at an *āmāśrāddha*, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall observe a penance for seven nights.
For eating the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal, one must fast for five nights.
If one eats the remnants of the food of a Kṣatriya, the penance lasts for three nights.
But for eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall fast for five nights.
One who eats the leavings of a Vaiśya shall fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra [becomes an outcaste].
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten prepared food [belonging to an outcaste], one must perform the Parāka penance.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, adhering to the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain incur death here and, after passing away, suffer the lack of atonement.
Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice by the Self-existent One himself;
for sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all, therefore, killing in sacrifice is not killing.
The sin incurred by a hunter seeking wealth does not compare to the sin that befalls one after death who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states of existence once again.
In the honey-mixture (madhuparka), at a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—
at these alone may animals be slain, and never elsewhere under any circumstances.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice,
leads both himself and those animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-controlled twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that violence toward the moving and non-moving beings which is ordained by the Veda and prescribed in this world is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure,
neither while living nor after death, shall ever find happiness.
He who does not desire to inflict the sufferings of bondage or death upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and toward whatever one forms an attachment—
that very thing one obtains without effort, provided one does not harm anything.
Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having thoroughly reflected upon the origin of meat, and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from the eating of all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the [prescribed] rule, like a *piśāca*,
becomes beloved in this world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dissects, the slayer, the buyer and seller,
the preparer, the server, and the eater— these are the killers.
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more demeritorious deeds than he.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by means of divine foods consisting of fruits and roots, nor by meals of the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh in this world shall eat me in the next world"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa).
One who has committed the theft of gold should present a mace to the king, confessing his deed.
By execution or by renunciation, one becomes purified.
One should observe the Mahāvrata for twelve years.
And one who misappropriates a deposit.
And one who steals grain or wealth must perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
For the theft of a human being, a woman, a well, a field, or a step-well, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed.
For goods of little value, the Sāntapana penance is prescribed.
For those who consume edible foods, drinks, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, and fruits, the penance is the drinking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should fast for three nights for consuming grass, wood, trees, dry food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one should eat only grains for twelve days.
In the case of stealing cotton, silk from insects, wool, and the like, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
(Viṣṇu Smṛti 52.11) In the case of stealing cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals, one should fast for two nights. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 52.12)
For the theft of birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one shall fast for a day.
Having restored by some means the property that was stolen from a creditor,
one should then perform an expiation for the removal of that taint.
Whatever a man who is unrestrained may take from others, by that very thing he shall be deprived when he is born again in whatever state of existence.
Since life, virtue, and desire are all established upon wealth,
one should therefore avoid the destruction of wealth with every possible effort.
He who is intent on harming living beings as well as intent on harming wealth incurs great suffering; of these two, the one intent on harming wealth suffers more.

Now, regarding sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, one shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year in the forest, wearing rags, according to the procedure for the Mahāvrata.
And for approaching the wife of another, [the penance is the same].
And for approaching a cow, one shall observe the *go-vrata*.

In the case of emission among males, in a non-vaginal opening, in empty space, in water, during the day, or while riding in a vehicle drawn by oxen, one should perform a bath along with one's clothes.
By having sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman, one shall attain equality with her.
If done through ignorance, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
And for sexual intercourse with a female animal or a prostitute, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
A woman who has once been corrupted by a man should perform that same vow which is prescribed for the man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
VisnuSm 54.01:
Whatever sinner associates with another, he shall perform that very person's penance.
Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-toed animal, or from one that is extremely defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
A Kṣatriya [should observe] two days.
A Vaiśya [should fast] for one day.
A Śūdra [should eat] at night.
And at the conclusion of the vow, everyone should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A Śūdra who drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor—
both of them go to the hell named Mahāraurava.
Except on festival days or when he is unwell, he who approaches his wife during her season shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
In the event of voiding urine or excrement where there is no water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One who has been overtaken by the rising sun or released after sunrise shall bathe with his clothes on and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one is bitten by a dog, a jackal, a village pig, a donkey, a monkey, a crow, or a woman, one should go to a river and perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
One who has extinguished the Vedic fires shall bathe three times a day, sleep on the ground, and subsist for one year by collecting alms only once a day.
For lying regarding one's own excellence, for persistent falsehood toward a teacher, and for reviling him, one shall subsist on milk alone for one month.
An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas—these shall subsist on alms for one year.

The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who marries before his elder, the woman with whom the younger brother marries, the giver of the bride, and the officiating priest—all these shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the Tapta-kṛcchra penance.

One who sells fresh herbs, perfumes, flowers, fruits, roots, skins, cane, split bamboo, husks, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, cow's milk, oil-cake, sesame seeds, or sesame oil shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.

One who sells substances derived from phlegm, lac, honey, food remnants, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, copper, or vessels made of rhinoceros horn, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells dyed cloth, dyes, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, liquids, or wool shall fast for three nights.
One who sells meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And he should initiate him once again.
Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, or having slept, or having eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month while staying in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
Having performed sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, having performed the funeral rites for others,
and having practiced malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) other than that directed against the low-born (*ahīna*), one removes these sins by means of three *kṛcchra* penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.

For those twice-born men who, having engaged in improper acts, desire to perform penance but have been excluded from the status of Brahmanahood— for them also, this [rite] should be prescribed as the first step.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation, they are purified by the renunciation of that wealth, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and austerity.
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, fasting is the expiation.
Having threatened [to strike] a Brahmin, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; for actually striking him, the *atikṛcchra*.

One should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances for causing blood to flow from a Brahmin. Once those who have committed offenses have been purified, one should not engage in any transaction with them whatsoever.
A knower of Dharma should not feel contempt for these persons once they have performed their ritual purification.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful— even if they have been purified according to the law— nor with those who kill those who seek refuge, nor with those who kill women.
One who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen,
as well as women and the sick, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 55:
Now, the secret expiations follow.

Having reached a flowing river and bathed, one who performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the prescribed characteristics every day and eats sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) once a day becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin within a month.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
By means of the vow and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, a drinker of spirituous liquor becomes purified.
One who has committed the theft of gold is purified by the recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.
One who has violated the preceptor’s bed is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-offerings of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of a twice-born man are consumed by breath control.
One should recite the Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, three times while restraining the breath;
that is called prāṇāyāma.
Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone,
Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out each quarter-verse of this Sāvitrī beginning with the word "tat."
A Brahmin learned in the Vedas who recites this syllable and this [Gāyatrī], preceded by the Vyāhṛtis,
at the two junctions of the day, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
Having recited this triad a thousand times outside [the village],
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
Deprived of these three, and failing to perform his own duties at the proper time,
a man of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya caste incurs censure among the virtuous.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable Om,
together with the three-footed Gāyatrī, should be known as the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath-control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic acts of offering oblations and performing sacrifices are perishable;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as both Brahman and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice performed according to ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña).
The whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundred times more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) a thousand times.
Those four types of *pākayajñas*, when combined with the *vidhiyajñas*,
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the *japayajña*.
A Brāhmaṇa attains perfection through the chanting of prayers alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, furthermore, there are the purifiers of all the Vedas.
Through the recitation of mantras and the performance of fire-offerings, those twice-born ones are purified from their sins.
The Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
That which is caused by the gods.
The Śuddhavatī verses.
The *Taratsamandīya* [Sāman].
The Kūṣmāṇḍa verses.
The Pāvamānī verses.
Durgā-Sāvitrī (VisnuSm 56-09)
Those who have extra limbs.
The *padas* and *stomas*. *Viṣṇu Smṛti* 56.11.
The Vyāhṛtis are equal [in length].
The Bhāruṇḍa birds.
The Candra-Sāman. VisnuSm 56-14.
The two Sāmans are Puruṣavrata.
The mark on the abdomen. VisnuSm 56-16ab.
The Bārhaspatya [is concluded]. VisnuSm 56-17.
VisnuSm 56-18: The Gō-sūkta.
The Aśva-sūkta (Horse-hymn) from Viṣṇu Smṛti 56.19a.
And the two Sāmans, as well as the Candra-sūkta.
The Śatarudriya (Viṣṇu Smṛti 56.21).
The Atharvaśiras. VisnuSm 56-22.
The Tri-suparṇa.
The Great Vow (mahā-vrata). VisnuSm 56-24.
The Nārāyaṇīya [section], ViṣṇuSm 56.25.
And the Puruṣasūkta.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these, when sung, purify living beings; and if one so desires, one attains the memory of former births.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 57: Now, those who are to be abandoned.
The Vrātyas. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 57.2)
They are outcasts.
They remain impure for three generations on both the mother's and the father's side.
All of these are indeed persons whose food should not be eaten and from whom gifts should not be accepted.
And one should avoid the practice of accepting gifts from those whose gifts should not be accepted.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic splendor of Brahmins perishes.
He who accepts a gift without knowing the rules for accepting various objects sinks down along with the giver.
And he who, though capable of receiving gifts, avoids receiving them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection from fear, meat, honey, a bed, a seat, a house, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered.
Prajāpati has declared that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, and not previously solicited, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats with contempt that [cow], nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblation.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he should not satisfy himself with those [gifts].
Even in these matters, though he may be capable of accepting gifts from them,
he shall not take [gifts] from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, nor likewise from an enemy.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept [gifts] from virtuous persons.
The partner in a business venture, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Now, for one in the householder stage of life, there are three kinds of wealth.
White, brindled, and black.
When one performs the funeral rites for the deceased with pure wealth, through that he attains divinity.
That which is mixed with the Śabala is human existence.
Whatever is done by a Kṛṣṇa [in this regard], that results in the state of being an animal.
That which is acquired by one's own means of livelihood is "white" for all.
That which is acquired through subsequent means is accompanied by strength.
And black iron that has been acquired through a single intermediate step [of trade] is also [forbidden].
Property inherited in due order, a gift out of affection, and what is acquired together with the wife—
all such wealth is declared to be "white" (pure) for all heirs without distinction.

That which is obtained through bribery or as a fee for a transaction involving what should not be sold, and that which is received from one who has rendered a service, is declared to be "tainted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through usury, gambling, theft, receiving gifts from improper persons, violence,
and fraud is declared to be "black" wealth.
Whatever a man performs with whatever kind of material substance, he obtains a corresponding fruit both after death and in this world.
A householder should perform the *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire.
The Agnihotra sacrifice is to be performed both in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities.
One should perform the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices at the times of the conjunction and the opposition of the moon and the sun, respectively.
The expiation is by means of a sacrificial animal.
And during the autumn and summer seasons, [one should sacrifice] with the Āgrayaṇa.
Or when rice and barley have been cooked.
We [possess] more than three years' supply.
Every year, [one should sacrifice] with the Soma.
In the absence of wealth, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.
Whatever wealth has been obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice, one should bestow it all entirely [upon the officiating priests].
One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation both in the evening and in the morning.
And one should give alms to a mendicant.
By giving alms to one who has been honored, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
In the absence of a mendicant, one should give even a mere mouthful of food to cows.
Or he may throw it into the fire.
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not refuse a mendicant.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiation for that, one should perform the sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and men.
The private recitation of one's own Vedic study is the Brahma-sacrifice.
The oblation offered to the gods is the *daiva*.
The libation to the ancestors is the ancestral rite.
The Bali offering is for the elementals (bhūtas).
The sacrifice to men consists of the honoring of guests.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder’s stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
Only the householder performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts; therefore, the one in the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, all living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
Having constantly practiced the pursuit of the three aims of life, the giving of food, the worship of the gods, the honoring of Brahmins, the study of one's own Veda,
and the libations to the ancestors, the householder goes to the station of Śakra.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, he should perform the voiding of urine and feces.
At night one should face south, during the day one should face north, and at the two twilights one should face east.
Not on ground that has not been covered.
Nor on ground that has been ploughed.
Nor in the shade.
Nor on saline soil.
Not on grassy ground.
Nor [should one eat] in the presence of living beings.
Nor in a pit.
Nor on an anthill.
Nor on a path.
Not on a carriage road.
Nor [should one study] when another person is impure.
Nor in a garden.
Nor should one study near a garden or a body of water.
Nor on ashes.
Nor on charcoal.
Nor on cow dung.
Nor in a cow-pen.
Nor in the open air.
Nor in water.
One should not look at the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a guru, or a Brāhmaṇa with the face turned away from them.
Nor indeed with his head uncovered.

Having wiped the anus with a clod of earth or a brick and having taken hold of the penis, one should rise and perform purification with water and earth drawn from a clean place until the odor and the smear are removed.
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand,
seven on both hands, and three on the two feet.
This is the purification for householders;
it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 61:
Now, one should not eat a tooth-stick made of palāśa wood.
Nor indeed [should one use wood] produced from the śleṣmātaka, ariṣṭa, vibhītaka, dhava, or dhanvana trees.
Nor [should one use wood] produced from the bandhūka, nirguṇḍī, śigru, tilva, or tinduka trees.
Nor [should one use wood] derived from the *kovidāra*, *samī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, or *guggulu* trees.
Nor [should one eat fruit] produced from the *pāribhadraka*, the *amlīkā*, the *mocaka*, the *śālmali*, or the *śaṇa*.
Nor that which is sweet.
Nor that which is sour.
Nor [should he eat] that which is dried out from the top.
Nor one that is hollow.
Nor that which has a foul odor.
Nor [should one eat] that which is slippery.
One should not face south or west.
And he should eat facing either the north or the east.
Any one of these: the *vaṭa*, *asana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *badara*, *sarja*, *nimba*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, or *bilva*.
Astringent, bitter, and pungent [tastes].

Having become pure at dawn and restrained in speech, one should consume the tooth-cleansing twig, which is twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and provided with a brush-like end.
Having rinsed it and broken it, one should carefully discard it in an impure place. One should never eat on the new moon day, nor should one ever use a tooth-stick on that day.
Now, for the twice-born, the sacred place (tīrtha) at the base of the little finger is named Prājāpatya.
The portion at the base of the thumb is sacred to Brahmā.
The offering to the gods is made at the tips of the fingers.
At the base of the index finger is the region of the ancestors (pitrya).

Seated in a clean place with his knees covered and facing either east or north, with his mind fixed on that [act] and his heart at peace, he should sip water that is not heated by fire, not frothy, not poured by a Śūdra or with only one hand, and not alkaline.
One should sip water three times with the *brāhma* tīrtha.
One should wipe twice.
One should touch the cavities, the head, and the heart with water.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified when the water merely touches the lips once.
VisnuSm 63.1:
Now, for the sake of acquisition and preservation, he should approach the Lord.
One should not set out on a journey alone.
Nor with those who are unrighteous.
Nor with Śūdras.
Nor with those who are enemies.
Nor at too early dawn.
Nor too late in the evening.
Not during the two twilights.
Not at midday.
Nor [should one eat] where water is not readily available.
Not too hurriedly.
Nor should one constantly travel with vehicles drawn by young animals, the sick, or those in distress.
Nor with those who have deficient limbs.
Nor with those who are distressed.
Nor with cows.
Nor with those who are not self-controlled.
Without first giving fodder and water to his draft animals, one should not satisfy one's own hunger and thirst.
One should not stand upon a crossroads.
Nor at the foot of a tree at night.
Nor should one enter an empty dwelling.
Nor even a blade of grass.
Nor [should one look at] a pen for tethering cattle.
One should not [step on] hair, husks, potsherds, bones, ashes, or charcoal.
Nor [should one eat] the seed-cotton of the cotton plant.
One should circumambulate a crossroads.
And [he should avoid] the image of a deity.
And [he should avoid] well-known trees.
And [he should see] fire, a Brāhmaṇa, a courtesan, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, the Vardhamāna, and the Nandyāvarta.
And [the sight of] a palm-leaf fan, a chowrie, a horse, an elephant, a goat, a cow, curd, milk, honey, and white mustard seeds.
And [he should avoid] the lute, sandalwood, weapons, fresh cow dung, fruits, flowers, fresh vegetables, gorocanā, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
And [the theft] of turbans, ornaments, gems, gold, silver, clothing, seats, vehicles, and foodstuffs.
Having seen a water-pot, a heap of grain, a bound animal, a young maiden, or a fish, one should proceed [on the path].
Now, having seen those who are intoxicated, insane, or deformed, one should turn back.
And those who have vomited, those who have been purged, those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and dwarfs.
And those wearing saffron robes, those who have renounced the world, and those who are filthy.
And [he may take] oil, molasses, dried cow-dung, fuel, grass, leafy twigs, ashes, and charcoal.
And [he shall not sell] salt, eunuchs, fermented liquors, hermaphrodites, cotton, ropes, fetters, and those with disheveled hair.
At the time of departure, one should greet with joy a lute, sandalwood, fresh vegetables, a turban, ornaments, and a young maiden.
One should not step upon the shadow of a deity, a Brāhmaṇa, a teacher, a tawny cow, or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
And [the water used for] spitting, vomit, blood, feces, urine, bathing, and washing; ViṣṇuSm 63.40.
One should not step over a calf's tethering rope.
One should not run while it is raining.
One should not cross a river in vain.
Nor [should one eat] without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors.
Nor with the two arms.
Nor with a cracked boat.
One should not stand upon a riverbank.
One should not look down into a well.
One should not step over it.
The way must be yielded to the elderly, the burdened, the king, one who has performed the ritual bath, a woman, the sick, a bridegroom, and those in vehicles;
however, among these, the king is not to yield the way to anyone else, nor shall one who has performed the ritual bath yield it to the king.
VisnuSm 64.01: One should not perform a ritual bath at water-reservoirs belonging to others.
In times of distress, one should perform [the rite] by extracting five lumps of earth and using water instead.
Nor when there is indigestion.
Nor one who is afflicted by illness.
Nor while naked.
Not at night.
Except during the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse).
Not during the two twilights.
One who is habituated to the morning bath should bathe upon seeing the eastern quarter, ruddy with the glow of dawn.
Having bathed, one should not shake one's head.
One should not draw up water from the limbs [of the body].
One should not touch [an object] smeared with oil.
One should not wear a garment previously worn that has not been washed first.
Having bathed, he should wear two washed garments along with a turban.
One should not engage in conversation with Mlecchas, Antyajas, or those who have fallen from their caste (patitas).
One should bathe in natural springs, in places excavated by deities, and in excellent lakes.

Water on the ground is more meritorious than water drawn up; flowing water is more meritorious than that which is stagnant; water received from a virtuous person is more meritorious than that; and water from the Gaṅgā is the most meritorious of all.

Having removed impurities with clay and water, and having immersed himself in the waters and sat down, he should consecrate the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*.
Then, submerged in water, he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Or [he may recite] "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
The Drupadā and the Sāvitrī.
Or he may recite the section beginning with "yuñjate manaḥ."
Or the Puruṣasūkta.
Having bathed and while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libation to the gods and ancestors while standing in water.
If he has changed his garment, he should do so after having stepped out of the water at a holy bathing place.
Without having performed the libations to the gods and ancestors, one should not wring out the bathing garment.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, he should touch [the organs] as prescribed.
One should offer flowers to Puruṣa with each verse of the Puruṣasūkta.
And [he should offer] handfuls of water.
At the very beginning, one should perform the libation for the gods using the "divine" (daiva) part of the hand.
Immediately after that, [the offering] for the ancestors is performed with the ancestral rite (pitrya).
Therein, first of all, one should perform the libation for those belonging to one's own lineage.
Then [the offering is made] to the relatives and kinsmen.
Then [the offering] to his friends.
In this manner, one should be a regular daily bather.
Having bathed, he should recite purificatory mantras according to his ability.
Especially the Sāvitrī.
And the Puruṣasūkta.
There is nothing superior to these two.
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purifying texts and for giving gifts as prescribed by the rules.
It is the firm conviction that misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams,
and evil thoughts perish for one who has been consecrated with merely water.
One who bathes daily does not behold the agonizing suffering of Yama’s realm;
indeed, even those men who are doers of evil are purified by the daily bath.

VisnuSm 65.1 Now, therefore, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should worship the Lord Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either in an image of a deity or on a consecrated spot.

Having offered the "taking of life" with the mantra, "Of the two Aśvins, the breaths; they [are] yours," and having performed the invocation with the anuvāka beginning with "They yoke the mind," he should perform a prostration with his knees, hands, and head.
One should present the *arghya* water with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
With the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," [he offers] water for the feet (pādya).
"May the waters of the desert be favorable to us"—with these words, water for sipping (ācamanīya) is offered.
"O Waters, carry away this [impurity]"—with these words, the water for bathing is offered.
On the chariot and on its axles, one should apply ointments and ornaments with the mantra "vṛṣabhasya vāje."
With the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," he puts on a garment.
"Flower-bearing" means flowers.
"Thou art the pole; drive away [evil]"—with these words, he offers incense.
"Thou art splendor; thou art semen"—with these words, [he offers] the lamp.
With the mantra "dadhi-krāvṇa," he offers the madhuparka.
The food offering is made with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇya-garbha."
The fly-whisk, the fan, the mirror, the umbrella, as well as the vehicle and the seat—
all that he should offer to the deity with the Sāvitra mantra alone.
Having thus worshipped, one should then recite the Puruṣasūkta;
with that very [mantra], one should offer oblations of clarified butter if one desires the eternal state.
VisnuSm 66.01: One should not perform rites for the gods or the ancestors with water that has been drawn at night.
One should not offer an unguent, except for sandalwood, musk, wood, camphor, saffron, and nutmeg.
Nor [should one wear] a garment dyed with indigo.
One must not wear an ornament that is an imitation of gems or gold.
Nor one who has a pungent odor.
Nor that which smells like a corpse.
Nor that which is produced from thorny plants.
One should offer even that which grows from thorns, provided it is white and fragrant.
One should also offer red saffron and that which is born in water.
One should not use living beings for the purpose of incense.
Nothing at all should be used for the purpose of a lamp except ghee or oil.
That which is unfit to be eaten is not to be used for the purpose of an offering.
Even among things that are otherwise edible, the milk of goats and buffaloes must not be consumed.
And the meat of five-clawed animals, fish, and boars.
Being self-restrained and pure, he should offer everything;
with his mind fixed on that [deity] and being well-disposed, he should be free from haste and anger.
VisnuSm 67.1:

Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, and poured water around it, he should take the first portion from all the cooked food and offer it as an oblation.
To Vāsudeva, to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, to Puruṣa, to Satya, to Acyuta, and to Vāsudeva.
Then [offerings] to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra and Agni together, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhanvantari, Vāstoṣpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, he should offer the bali-oblation with the remainder of the food.
By means of the primary food and the secondary food.
On all sides, [he should place them] to the east of the fire.
For all [the cows], he says: "Thou art named Ambā," "Thou art named Dulā," "Thou art named Nitantī," and "Thou art named Cupuṇīkā."
"Nandini, Subhage, Sumaṅgali, Bhadraṅkarī"—with these words, he circumambulates his daughters-in-law from left to right.
To Sthūṇā, to Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the Vanaspatis.
At the gateway between righteousness and unrighteousness, and unto death.
To Varuṇa, at the water-vessel.
"To Viṣṇu" [is the offering] at the mortar.
With the words "To the Maruts," [he offers] upon the lower grinding stone.
Above, one should offer to King Vaiśravaṇa and to the spirits (bhūtas).
"To Indra and to the attendants of Indra"—thus [one offers] in the eastern half.
"To Yama and to the messengers of Yama," [he offers] in the southern half.
"To Varuṇa and to the attendants of Varuṇa"—thus [he offers] in the western half.
"To Soma, to the men of Soma"—thus [he offers] in the northern half.
"To Brahmā and to the attendants of Brahmā," [he says] in the middle.
Above, [the offering] is for Ākāśa.
On a sacrificial mound, one should offer [oblations] during the day with the words, "To the beings who roam by day."
"To those who roam at night" means at night.

Then, upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, he should perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, as well as for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, by means of their names and *gotras*.
He should also offer ointments, flowers, incense, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, to the rice balls.
Having placed a water-pitcher nearby, he should cause the recitation of a benediction.
One should offer [the food] upon the ground for one's own dogs, crows, and outcaste dogs.
And one should give alms.
And one should exert the greatest effort in honoring guests.
One should diligently honor a guest who arrives in the evening.
One should not allow a hungry guest to dwell in one's house.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes and as the husband is the lord of women, so is the guest the lord of the householder.
By worshipping him, one attains heaven.
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated,
he takes away that person’s merit and bestows his own demerit upon him.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally known as a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.
One should not consider a Brahmin who is a resident of the same village, nor one who is merely a casual acquaintance,
as a guest when he has arrived at the house, even if his wife or the sacred fires are present there.
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the manner of a guest,
he too may be fed at will after the Brahmins have finished their meal.
Even when a Vaiśya or a Śūdra arrive at the household as guests,
he should feed them along with his servants, practicing compassion toward them.
He should, together with his wife, feed according to his ability with ordinary food those others as well— such as friends and so forth— who have come to his house out of affection.
One should feed a woman living in one's own home, a maiden, a sick woman, and likewise a pregnant woman, before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [deities] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, as well as his own servants, have finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains.
Having worshipped the gods, the ancestors, human beings, dependents, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remnants.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of the remnants of a sacrifice.
A householder does not attain such worlds through his own Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or asceticism as he does through the honoring of guests.
In the evening and in the morning, one should provide a seat and water to a guest,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored them in accordance with the prescribed rule.
By giving shelter, as well as a bed, oil for massaging the feet, and a lamp— each gift individually— one obtains a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat.
Having bathed, one should eat when the two [the sun and the moon] have been released [from eclipse].
When the two [the sun and the moon] have set without having been released [from eclipse], one should bathe and look at them on the following day.
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, nor when cows or Brahmins are afflicted.
Nor during a calamity of the king.
When one who has gone abroad considers the Agnihotra sacrifice to have been performed, then he may eat.
When he considers that the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has indeed been performed.
And when one considers that a lunar festival (parvan) has occurred on the day of the full moon or new moon, [that too is a time for offering].
And one should not eat while the previous meal is undigested.
Not at midnight.
Nor during the midday meal.
Nor during the two twilights.
Nor [should one study] while wearing wet clothes.
One should not wear only a single garment.
Nor while naked.
Nor in water.
One should not study while squatting on the heels.
Nor [should one eat] while seated on a broken seat.
Nor [should one study] while lying on a bed.
Nor at a meal where the food has been broken apart.
Nor on one's lap.
Not on the ground.
Nor on the hand.
And where one might offer salt, that [food] one should not eat.
One should not revile children.
One person alone shall not eat choice food.
Nor [should one eat] that from which the oil has not been removed.
One should not eat parched grains during the day.
One should not [perform] any rite involving sesame seeds at night.
Nor curd-mixed barley meal.
One should not [use] the wood of the *kovidāra*, *vaṭa*, *pippala*, *śāṇa*, or *śāka* trees.
Not without having given [the portion]. Viṣṇu Smṛti 68.32.
One should not [eat] without having offered oblations.
One should not [enter] with unwetted feet.
And one should not [recite] with hands and face unwashed.
One should not take ghee while still impure from food remnants.
One should not gaze at the moon, the sun, or the stars.
One should not touch the head.
One should not recite the Veda.
One should eat facing the east.
Or he may face the south.
Having honored the food.
He should be cheerful, wearing a garland and anointed with unguents.
One should not consume [the food] until it is completely finished.
Except for curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, parched grain flour, and sweetmeat balls.

One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in an open space, nor likewise while standing up; nor should many eat together while many look on, nor should many eat together while looking at a single person.
One should never drink water from one's cupped hands (añjali) in an empty house, in a fire-sanctuary, or in a temple; nor should one practice excessive satiety.

One should not eat a third meal, nor anything unwholesome under any circumstances; one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor having eaten in the evening, should one eat again in the morning.
One should not eat food that is defiled in intention, nor from a vessel defiled in intention;
nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth around the knees.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 69:
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, one should not approach a woman.
Nor after having eaten at a śrāddha.
Nor having given [it].
One should not fail to accept an invitation to a śrāddha ceremony.
One who observes a vow [should not do so].
Nor one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
Nor in temples of the gods, cremation grounds, or deserted dwellings.
Nor at the roots of trees.
Not during the day.
Not during the two twilights.
Nor one who is soiled.
One who is not impure [should perform the rites].
Nor one who is anointed with oil.
Nor [should he eat] while anointed with oil.
Nor one who is afflicted by disease.
One who is afflicted by disease [is not qualified].
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in limbs, nor one with redundant limbs, nor likewise one who is advanced in age,
nor a woman who is pregnant.
One should not sleep with wet feet.
One should not have one's head toward the north or the west.
Nor while naked.
Nor [should one recite] the genealogical hymn (anuvamśa).
Nor in the open air.
Nor on a palāśa tree, nor on a bed.
Nor [should one eat] from that which is made of the five kinds of wood.
Nor for that which has been broken by an elephant.
Nor [is it impure] when caused by lightning or fire.
Not on a cracked [vessel].
Nor on the back of a fire.
Nor [should one eat] from that which grows on a tree watered by a jar.
Nor in cremation grounds, deserted dwellings, or temples dedicated to deities.
Nor among fickle women.
Nor [should one study] in the midst of women.
Nor [should one step] over grain, cattle, a teacher, fire, or the gods.
One should not sleep while impure from food remnants, nor during the day, nor at the two twilights, nor on ashes;
nor in an impure place, nor on moist ground, nor on the peak of a mountain.
VisnuSm 71: Now, one should not despise anyone at all.
And one should not mock those who have missing or extra limbs, nor fools, nor those destitute of wealth.
One should not serve those who are inferior.
One should not perform any action that is contrary to one's own sacred study.
One should adopt an attire appropriate to one's age.
Of sacred learning, noble lineage, wealth, and country.
One should not be arrogant.
One should constantly study the scriptures and other such works.
When wealth is available, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
One should not say, "It does not exist."
One should not wear a garland that is scentless, foul-smelling, or red.
One may wear even a red lotus.
And a staff made of bamboo.
And a water-pot containing water.
The sacred thread shall be made of cotton.
And two earrings made of gold.
One should not look at the rising sun.
Nor [should one eat] when the sun is setting.
Nor [should one eat] what is covered by a cloth.
Nor [should one look at] that which is situated within a mirror or in water.
Not at midday.
One should not look at the face of an angry teacher.
One should not look at one's own reflection in oil or water.
Nor [should one look at oneself] in a mirror that is soiled with dirt.
One should not [invite] one's wife at the time of eating.
Nor a naked woman.
Nor [should he look at] anyone while they are urinating.
Nor [should one look at] an elephant that has broken loose from its tethering post.
And one who is in a precarious position shall not engage in a fight with bulls or other such animals.
Nor one who is insane. VisnuSm 71.30.
Nor one who is intoxicated. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 71.31)
One should not throw impure substances into the fire.
Nor blood. VisnuSm 71.33.
Not poison. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 71.34)
Also [the impurity of] water.
One should not step over the fire.
One should not warm one's feet [over a fire].
One should not wipe oneself with *kuśa* grass.
One should not clean [the teeth] with a vessel made of bell-metal.
One should not place one foot upon the other.
One should not draw a figure of the earth.
One should not be a crusher of clods of earth.
One should not be a cutter of grass.
One should not clip one's nails or hair with the teeth.
And one should avoid gambling.
Nor should one expose oneself to the heat of the sun while still a child.
One should not wear garments, sandals, garlands, or sacred threads that have been worn by another.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra.
Neither the leavings of food nor the sacrificial oblation [should be given to a dog].
Nor sesame seeds.
And one should not instruct him in the Dharma.
VisnuSm 71-52: There is no vow [in this case].
One should not scratch one's head or belly with both hands joined together.
One should not refuse curd or flowers.
One should not pull at one's own garland.
One should not awaken one who is sleeping.
One should not cause a red garment to fade.
One should not speak to a woman in her courses.
Nor [should one eat with] Mlecchas or those born of the lowest castes (antyaja).
In the presence of the fire, the deity, and the Brahmins, he should raise his right hand.
One should not point out a cow grazing in another's field.
Nor one who is drinking [milk] from its calf.
One should not cause those who have not been elevated to exult.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra.
Nor in a place crowded with unrighteous people.
One should not dwell with one who is devoid of medical knowledge.
Nor when [the sun] has not yet risen.
Nor for long on a mountain.
One should not engage in useless exertion.
Nor [should one eat] while dancing or singing. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 71.70)
One should not snap one's fingers.
One should not utter vulgar speech.
VisnuSm 71–73: Not untruth.
One should not do what is displeasing to Viṣṇu.
One should not strike anyone at their vital points.
One who desires to live a long life should not despise oneself.
One should perform the twilight worship for a long time.
One should not play with snakes or weapons.
One should not touch the bodily apertures without a specific cause.
One should not raise a staff against another.
One should strike him for the purpose of correction.
One should strike him on the back with a bamboo leaf or with a rope.
One should avoid speaking ill of gods, Brahmins, the scriptures, and great-souled beings.
And wealth and pleasure that are contrary to righteousness [should not be pursued].
And even a dharma that is loathed by the world [should not be practiced].
And on the festival days (parvan), one should perform propitiatory oblations (śānti-homa).
One should not cut even a blade of grass.
And he should remain adorned with ornaments.
Thus one should be a follower of right conduct.

One who desires righteousness and has conquered his senses should practice that conduct which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, which is consistent with dharma, and which is practiced by the virtuous.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired goal;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and through right conduct, one destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is endowed with faith, and is free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
VisnuSm 72.01: He should abide with self-restraint and self-control.
And self-restraint of the senses is proclaimed as *dama*.
This world and the next belong to the self-controlled man.
No ritual action of one who is not self-controlled ever succeeds.
Self-restraint is the supreme purifier; self-restraint is the supreme auspiciousness. Through self-restraint, one obtains everything that one desires in the mind.
If the horses do not carry away that chariot—yoked with five [steeds], moving at the speed of thought, and following the noble path—then they do not fail him who has gone thus. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 72.6)
Just as the waters enter the ocean—which is ever-filling and established in immovability—so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
VisnuSm 73.1:
Now, one who desires to perform a śrāddha should invite the Brāhmaṇas on the day before.

On the second day, in the forenoon during the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) and in the afternoon during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa), he should cause the Brahmins—who have bathed well and sipped water (svācānta)—to sit upon seats covered with Kuśa grass, arranged according to their seniority in age.
Two [brāhmaṇas] for the rite to the gods, facing east, and three for the rite to the ancestors, facing north.
"One by one on both occasions," or "alternately."
In the case of *āmaśrāddhas* and those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should offer oblations into the fire using the first five [verses] of the hymn.
In the *paśu-śrāddhas*, [one should offer] with the middle five [verses].
On the new moon days, [one should perform the rite] with the excellent group of five [days].
After the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon, on the eighth days of the dark fortnights, one should perform the rites in sequence with the first, middle, and highest sets of five [verses].
And also on the days following the Aṣṭakās.
Then, having received permission from the Brāhmaṇas, he should invoke the ancestors.
Having performed the dismissal of the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds while reciting the two verses beginning with "apayantu asurāḥ," [he should proceed].

Having performed the invocation with the mantra, "O Pitṛs, may all of you come here first to me; this is for you, O Pitṛs," and having offered water for washing the feet (pādya) mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds using fragrant water with the mantras "yās tiṣṭhanti amṛtā vāk" and "yan me mātā," and having prepared and offered the *arghya*, and having applied unguents, he should honor the Brahmins according to his ability with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps, and then take food soaked in ghee.
Having looked at them and said, "The Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus—may I perform [this] in the fire," and having been told by the Brahmins, "Do so," he should offer three oblations.

Having performed the consecration of the oblation with the mantras, "O my ancestors, this is for you, O ancestors, this is the sacrifice," he should first present the food to the two facing east, saying, "Salutation to all the gods (viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ)," placing it especially in vessels made of silver as they are available.
To the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, [one should offer] by means of their names and lineages (gotra) to those facing north.
While the Brahmins are eating that [food], he should mutter: "Whatever [sin] I have committed through excess, by day and by night, O you who eat raw flesh."
And the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 73.16)
In the vicinity of the remnants, upon kusa grass with the tips pointing southward, he should place one pinda for the father, reciting: "The earth is an inexhaustible ladle."
"Antarikṣaṃ darvir akṣitā" (The atmosphere is the imperishable ladle)—with these words, he offers the second pinda to the grandfather.
"dyaur darvir akṣitā" (the sky is the inexhaustible ladle)—with this verse, the third [offering] is for the great-grandfather.
"O ancestors who have passed away here," with these words, a garment should be given.
The food [is offered with the mantra]: "O ancestors, bestow heroic food. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 73.21)
"O ancestors, rejoice here according to your respective portions"—with these words, he rubs his hands at the base of the *darbha* grass.

Having performed the scattering of water around the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) clockwise while reciting the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," he should present the water-offering (argha), flowers, incense, unguents, food, and other kinds of edibles and delicacies.
And a water-vessel combined with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.

When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, he should sprinkle the food along with the grass blades with the mantra "May you not perish for me" (mā me kṣeṣthāḥ), and having placed the scattered remnants of food before the leavings, he should ask, "Are you satisfied? Is it well-prepared? Then, having first given water for sipping (ācamana) to those facing north, and then to those facing east, and then having sprinkled the site of the Śrāddha with the words "Well-sprinkled" (suprokṣitam), he, holding Darbha grass in his hand, should perform all the remaining rites.

Then, having circumambulated [the image] from the front while facing east, reciting "yan me rāma," and having returned, he should honor them with sacrificial fees according to his ability, say, "May you be pleased," and when they have replied, "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra, "The gods and the ancestors."

Having offered the water for imperishability (*akṣayya-udaka*) by means of the names and lineages (*nāma-gotra*), he should then, with palms joined and mind fixed on that, with a well-disposed heart, request from those facing east: "May the Viśvedevas be pleased."
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
They should say, "So be it."
May we have abundant food, and may we receive guests;
may there be those who solicit us, and may we never have to solicit anyone.
Having received these blessings with these two [verses], ViṣṇuSm 73.31.
Then, having honored the Brahmins according to the rule, followed them, and saluted them, he should dismiss them with the mantra "vāje vāje."

Viṣṇu Smṛti 74.1: Having performed the *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakā* days preceded by offerings to the gods with vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire on the subsequent *aṣṭakās* (the *anvaṣṭakās*) as on the *aṣṭakā* days, one should likewise feed the Brahmins for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, preceded by offerings to the gods; then, having honored them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should follow them and bid them farewell.
Then one should make trenches.
At its base, having performed the kindling of the fire toward the east, north, and south, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is made.
At the base of three furrows for the males, and at the base of three furrows for the females.
One should fill three pits for the man with water mixed with food.
For a woman, three trenches filled with milk and food [should be prepared].
With curd, meat, and milk, one should [fill] three trenches respectively.
Having filled [the vessel], he should recite this: "May this be inexhaustible for you, O venerable sirs, and for you, O venerable ladies."
VisnuSm 75.01:
While the father is alive, he who performs a śrāddha should perform it for those for whom his father would perform it.
Those whose grandfather is living while both their father and paternal grandfather are alive.
While the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather are all living, one must not perform [the rite] at all.
If one's father should be deceased, he, having placed the rice-ball for the father, should offer [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather.
He whose father and grandfather are deceased should, having offered two pindas to them, offer [one] to his great-grandfather.
He whose grandfather has died should, having placed a rice-ball for him, offer [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the great-grandfather.

In the same manner, a wise man should perform the śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers; he should do so according to the rule by adapting the mantras, while for the remaining ancestors it is performed without mantras.

The new moon day, the three Aṣṭakās, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the full moon day of Māgha, the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following that, and the times of the ripening of rice and barley.
Prajāpati has declared these times for the śrāddha to be obligatory;
one who does not perform the śrāddha on these occasions falls into hell.
VisnuSm 77: The transit of the sun.
VisnuSm 77-01. The transit of the sun.
The two equinoxes.
Especially so during the two solstices.
The Vyatīpāta [yoga].
The birth asterism.
And there shall be prosperity.
Prajāpati has indeed declared these to be the optional times for the śrāddha;
whatever śrāddha is given on these occasions conduces to infinity.
A wise person should certainly not perform a śrāddha during the two twilights or at night;
however, even during those times, it may be performed if there is an eclipse of the moon or sun.
For a śrāddha offered at the time of an eclipse of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire.
One who constantly performs a śrāddha on a Sunday obtains good health.
Good fortune is obtained through the moon.
On a Tuesday, one obtains victory in battle.
All desires [are fulfilled] at the Bodhi [tree].
One should study the desired science during the period of Jupiter.
Wealth [is obtained] from Venus.
Life [is gained] when Saturn is present.
In Kṛttikā, one attains heaven.
Offspring are obtained under the asterism Rohiṇī.
In the Saumya [oblation], there is the attainment of spiritual luster.
Success in ritual action is attained through the Raudra [mantra].
One should plow the earth under the asterism Punarvasu.
One should perform the rite for nourishment under the Puṣya asterism.
In the case of a snake, [one obtains] prosperity.
One obtains all desires at the rite for the ancestors.
Good fortune [is assigned] to the Bhāgya [nakṣatra].
In the case of recovering wealth, [the interest shall be] at the rate of one-eighth.
The preeminence among kinsmen is in the hand.
In the sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ, one obtains daughters endowed with beauty.
Success in trade is attained under Svāti.
Gold [should be offered] under the Viśākhā constellation.
Friends [should be invited] for a rite dedicated to Mitra.
The kingdom [is established] in Śakra.
Agriculture [is the livelihood] for the Mūla [division].
Success in sea voyages [is attained] when the moon is in the sign of Aquarius.
In the Vaiśvadeva rite, one indeed obtains all desires.
Supremacy is attained through the Abhijit constellation.
Upon hearing [this], one obtains all desires.
Salt, [if stolen], [is expiated] during the month of Vāsava.
Good health is obtained through the Vāruṇa [oblation].
Base metals [are to be given] at a sacrifice.
The house is the womb of the earth.
One should give cows under the asterism of Puṣya.
Horses [should be offered] to Aśvinī.
Life [is obtained] in the southern quarter.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), women of beautiful form [should enter] the house.
On the second lunar day, one should worship Kanyā, who bestows boons.
On the third lunar day, one obtains all desires.
On the fourth [lunar day], one should sacrifice animals.
On the fifth [lunar day], one obtains handsome sons.
Victory in gambling on the sixth lunar day.
One should engage in agriculture on the seventh lunar day.
Trade on the eighth day.
On the ninth day, [one should sacrifice] animals.
Horses [should be sacrificed] on the tenth day.
On the eleventh day, one obtains sons endowed with spiritual luster.
Gold and silver [should be given] on the twelfth day.
On the thirteenth lunar day, one attains good fortune.
One obtains all desires on the fifteenth day.
For those killed by weapons, the fourteenth day is prescribed for the performance of the śrāddha rite.
There are also two verses sung by the ancestors:
"May there arise in our lineage some preeminent man who,
being composed, [performs this] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight during the rainy season."

VisnuSm 79.1 Now, one should not perform a śrāddha with water taken at night.
In the absence of *kuśa* grass, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* grass in place of the *kuśa*.
For the purpose of clothing, thread made from cotton [is used].
One should discard the fringe, even if it is made of unwashed cloth.
Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those produced from thorny plants [should not be offered].
One should offer white, fragrant flowers—even those grown on thorny plants—and also red aquatic flowers.
One should not offer fat or marrow for the purpose of a lamp.
One should offer either clarified butter or oil.
One should not offer any animal-derived substance for the purpose of incense.
One should offer guggulu mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of unguents.
One should not give salt that is visible [to the recipient].
And one should eat ghee, vegetables, and so forth with the hand.
One should give metallic vessels as gifts.
Especially those made of silver.
One should place a sword, a kutapa blanket, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains—these being purifying and destructive of demons.

One should avoid long pepper (*pippalī*), *mukundaka*, *bhūstṛṇa*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), *surasā*, *sarjaka*, *suvarcala*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, bottle gourd (*alābu*), eggplant (*vārtāka*), *pālakyā*, water spinach (*upodakī*), *taṇḍulīyaka*, safflower (*kusumbha*), yam (*piṇḍāluka*), and buffalo milk (*mahiṣī-kṣīra*).
Rājamāṣa beans, lentils, food that has stood overnight, and prepared salts.
One should avoid anger.
One should not shed tears.
One should not act with haste.
VisnuSm 79.22: For the gift of clarified butter and other substances, vessels made of precious metals, swords as vessels, and vessels of inferior metal are recommended.
And on this point, there is a verse:
A gift given with vessels made of gold or silver, or with one of steel or udumbara wood, or even with a vessel of bell-metal, attains imperishability.
With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, śyāmāka grain, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, mung beans, and wheat, [the ancestors] are gratified for one month.
For two months, [one should subsist] on fish meat.
Three [cows] with the meat of a black antelope.
And four [days] with the meat of a sheep.
Five [cubits] with the measure of a bird.
Six [cows] for a goat.
Seven [days] with the Raurava [Sāman].
Eight [cows] with the meat of a spotted deer.
[One becomes pure] by [drinking] the water of nine cows.
Ten [cows] with the meat of a buffalo.
But with a hornless goat, [the sacrifice] is elevenfold.
For one year, he should subsist on cow's milk or its products.
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
We eat black vegetables, large-scaled fish, the meat of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane,
and rhinoceroses— excluding those with horns— as long as the sun endures.
One should not place food upon a seat.
One should not touch [it] with the foot.
One should not sneeze while facing downwards.
One should drive away the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) with sesame seeds or mustard seeds.
And one should perform the śrāddha in an enclosed place.
One should not look at a woman who is menstruating.
Nor a dog.
Nor [the meat of] a village pig.
Nor should one eat a village cock.
One should diligently present the śrāddha offering to the Unborn (Ajasya).
And the Brahmins, restrained in speech, should eat.
Nor [should one eat] with the head wrapped [in a cloth].
Nor [should they eat] while wearing sandals.
Nor [should one eat] with the feet placed upon a seat.
Those with missing limbs or extra limbs must not look upon the śrāddha.
Śūdras [are not entitled to this]. VisnuSm 81-16.
They are not outcasts.
Nor [should one give] to those who are chronically ill.
At that time, he should honor a Brāhmaṇa or a mendicant with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
When asked by the giver, the Brāhmaṇas should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is steam from the food, as long as those who eat remain silent,
and as long as the qualities of the oblation have not been described, so long do the ancestors eat.
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground before those who have finished eating.
For women of the family who have died without having received the sacraments,
or who have been abandoned, their allotted share shall be the food left on the dishes and that which is scattered upon the *darbha* grass.
The remnants of food that have fallen upon the ground at a rite for the ancestors (pitrya) are declared to be the share of the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit.
VisnuSm 82.01: In rites for the gods, one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa.
One should examine [the suitability of the recipient] with great care in rites for the ancestors.
One should avoid those who have missing or extra limbs.
And those who persist in improper actions.
Those who observe the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika).
Those who wear the marks of religious orders in vain.
Those who subsist by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra).
And [one should avoid] those who serve the gods for a livelihood (devalakas).
Physicians. VisnuSm 82-09.
The sons of unmarried women.
His sons. VisnuSm 82-11.
Those who perform many sacrifices.
Those who officiate as priests for an entire village.
Those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
Those who perform sacrifices for persons for whom one should not sacrifice.
The Vrātyas. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 82.16)
Those who sacrifice for him [become outcastes].
Those who cause the performance of religious festivals (parvakāraḥ).
Those who give hints. VisnuSm 82-19.
Those who teach for a fee. Visnusmṛti 82.20.
Those taught by a paid teacher (VisnuSm 82.21).
Those nourished by the food of a Śūdra.
From associating with those who have fallen [from their caste].
Those who do not study [the Veda].
Those who have fallen away from the performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
[The rules concerning] the king's servants. VisnuSm 82-26.
Nor those who are naked. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 82.27)
Those who are disputing with their father.
And those who abandon their father, mother, teacher, the sacred fire, or their own Vedic study; ViṣṇuSm 82.29.
For these are declared to be outcasts among Brāhmaṇas, defilers of the assembly;
a wise man should avoid them with effort during the performance of a Śrāddha rite.
Visnu Smṛti 83: Now, those who purify the company at a meal (paṅktipāvanas).
One who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice.
One who maintains the five fires.
One who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
One who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Or one who has mastered even a single auxiliary science (aṅga) of the Veda.
One who has mastered the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and Grammar.
He should also have mastered one treatise on Dharmaśāstra.
Purified by a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Purified by sacrifice. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 83.10)
Purified by austerity.
Purified by truth.
Purified by the mantra (ViṣṇuSm 83.13).
One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
The lineage of that which was given as a *brahmadeya* [is exempt from partition].
The Trisuparṇa. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 83.16)
The son-in-law. VisnuSm 83-17.
And the daughter's son is also a worthy recipient.
And especially so for a yogin.
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
"May he also be born in our family who,
with great effort, feeds a yogi— a Brahmin at a śrāddha— by which we ourselves may be satisfied."
VisnuSm 84.

One should not go to a region inhabited by Mlecchas.
"Having drunk water at the drinking-troughs of others, one attains equality with them," so it is said.
That region in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a Mleccha country; beyond that is Āryāvarta.

In this very same manner, [the rite is performed] at Gayāśīrṣa.
At a banyan tree.
On Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
On Mount Varāha.

At Kuśāvarta.

On Mount Nīla.

At Bhṛgutuṅga.
